credit: tr. in The World's Famous Orations, ed. William Jennings Bryan, 1906 (translator not named)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: mary-shelley
text: Everywhere I see bliss, from which I alone am irrevocably excluded. I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend.
work: Frankenstein (1818), ch. 10
note: spoken by the creature to his maker

speaker: maimonides
text: We are like those who, though beholding frequent flashes of lightning, still find themselves in the thickest darkness of the night.
work: The Guide for the Perplexed, introduction

speaker: hippocrates
text: Into whatever houses I enter, I will go into them for the benefit of the sick, and will abstain from every voluntary act of mischief and corruption…
work: The Oath
note: the oath of the physicians of his school, traditionally ascribed to him

speaker: horatio-nelson
text: It is warm work, and this day may be the last to any of us at a moment…
work: At the Battle of Copenhagen, 1801
note: Southey's account

speaker: cyrus-the-great
text: Vice, passing lightly along her path of pleasure, wins the hearts of thousands with her gifts; but Virtue, toiling up the steep ascent, has little skill to snare the souls of men and draw them after her…
work: Xenophon, Cyropaedia, book 2
note: Xenophon's account, in his idealised life of Cyrus

speaker: marco-polo
text: …and People of all degrees who desire to get knowledge of the various races of mankind and of the diversities of the sundry regions of the World, take this Book and cause it to be read to you.
work: Travels, prologue
credit: tr. Henry Yule, 1871 (3rd ed., rev. Henri Cordier, 1903)
note: written down by Rustichello of Pisa from his telling

speaker: thurgood-marshall
text: …it means that a State has no business telling a man, sitting alone in his own house, what books he may read or what films he may watch.
work: Stanley v. Georgia (1969), opinion of the Supreme Court
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: maximilien-robespierre
text: If virtue be the spring of a popular government in times of peace, the spring of that government during a revolution is virtue combined with terror: virtue, without which terror is destructive; terror, without which virtue is impotent.
work: Report on the Principles of Political Morality, February 1794

speaker: baruch-spinoza
text: Blessedness is not the reward of virtue, but virtue itself; neither do we rejoice therein, because we control our lusts, but, contrariwise, because we rejoice therein, we are able to control our lusts.
work: Ethics, part 5, proposition 42

speaker: hannibal
text: Alexander, king of Macedonia; because, with a small band, he defeated armies whose numbers were beyond reckoning; and because he had overrun the remotest regions, the merely visiting of which was a thing above human aspiration.
work: Livy, History of Rome, book 35
note: his answer at Ephesus when Scipio Africanus asked him who was the greatest general; Livy takes the story from the annalist Claudius, who had it from Acilius

speaker: lili-uokalani
text: Oh, honest Americans, as Christians hear me for my down-trodden people! Their form of government is as dear to them as yours is precious to you. Quite as warmly as you love your country, so they love theirs.
work: Hawaii's Story by Hawaii's Queen (1898), on the proposed annexation
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: lorenzo-valla
text: I know that for a long time now men’s ears are waiting to hear the offense with which I charge the Roman pontiffs.
work: On the Forged Donation of Constantine (1440)

speaker: johannes-kepler
text: What have plane figures to do with solid orbits? Solid bodies ought to be used for solid orbits.
work: On his search for the order of the planets, c. 1595 (Brewster, The Martyrs of Science)
note: as David Brewster quotes him

speaker: isaac-newton
text: My Design in this Book is not to explain the Properties of Light by Hypotheses, but to propose and prove them by Reason and Experiments…
work: Opticks (1704), book 1, opening

speaker: david
text: The beauty of Israel is slain upon thy high places: how are the mighty fallen!
work: 2 Samuel 1:19, his lament for Saul and Jonathan
note: the lament as the Second Book of Samuel gives it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: julia-ward-howe
text: Mine eyes have seen the glory of the coming of the Lord: He is trampling out the vintage where the grapes of wrath are stored; He hath loosed the fateful lightning of His terrible swift sword: His truth is marching on.
work: Battle Hymn of the Republic (The Atlantic Monthly, 1862)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: antonio-pigafetta
text: …we only ate old biscuit reduced to powder, and full of grubs, and stinking from the dirt which the rats had made on it when eating the good biscuit, and we drank water that was yellow and stinking.
work: Account of Magellan's voyage: crossing the Pacific, 1520-1521

speaker: montesquieu
text: Liberty is a right of doing whatever the laws permit; and if a citizen could do what they forbid, he would no longer be possest of liberty, because all his fellow citizens would have the same power.
work: The Spirit of Laws, book 11, chapter 3
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: aristotle
text: …men come to be builders, for instance, by building; harp-players, by playing on the harp: exactly so, by doing just actions we come to be just; by doing the actions of self-mastery we come to be perfected in self-mastery; and by doing brave actions brave.
work: Nicomachean Ethics, book 2

speaker: daniel-oconnell
text: I am for leaving England to the English, Scotland to the Scotch; but we must have Ireland for the Irish.
work: Speech at Mullaghmast for the repeal of the Union, 1843
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: elizabeth-cady-stanton
text: We come into the world alone, unlike all who have gone before us; we leave it alone under circumstances peculiar to ourselves.
work: The Solitude of Self, address to the House Judiciary Committee (1892)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: isidore-of-seville
text: For among the ancients no one wrote history unless he had been present and witnessed what was to be described. For we understand what we see better than we do what we gather by hearsay.
work: Etymologies, book 1, chapter 41 (On history)

speaker: isaiah
text: …they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
work: Isaiah 2:4
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: wang-anshi
text: For learning in these days is a totally different pursuit from what it was in the olden times; and it is now impossible otherwise to get at the real meaning of our ancient sages.
work: Letter to a friend on the study of false doctrines (in Giles, A History of Chinese Literature)

speaker: jeremiah
text: The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved.
work: Jeremiah 8:20
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: david-hume
text: Custom, then, is the great guide of human life. It is that principle alone which renders our experience useful to us, and makes us expect, for the future, a similar train of events with those which have appeared in the past.
work: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, section 5

speaker: susan-b-anthony
text: It was we, the people, not we, the white male citizens, nor yet we, the male citizens, but we, the whole people, who formed this Union.
work: Is It a Crime for a Citizen of the United States to Vote?, speech of 1873
note: as printed in the History of Woman Suffrage, volume 2 (1882)

speaker: homer
text: There is one omen, and one only—that a man should fight for his country.
work: Iliad, book 12
note: spoken by Hector

speaker: zhu-xi
text: …it was quite a joke to see how accurately he reproduced my coarse ugly face and my vulgar rustic turn of mind…
work: Testimonial for the portrait painter Kuo Kung-chen (in Giles, A History of Chinese Literature)

speaker: mary-wollstonecraft
text: It is time to effect a revolution in female manners, time to restore to them their lost dignity, and make them, as a part of the human species, labour by reforming themselves to reform the world.
work: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), chapter 3

speaker: hesiod
text: Work is no disgrace: it is idleness which is a disgrace.
work: Works and Days

speaker: ulysses-s-grant
text: No terms except an unconditional and immediate surrender can be accepted. I propose to move immediately upon your works.
work: Letter to General Buckner at Fort Donelson, 16 February 1862
note: as printed in his Personal Memoirs (1885)

speaker: yue-fei
text: Such is the capacity for endurance in those who are well fed and well treated; who are willing, but not over-zealous.
work: Good Horses, his answer to the emperor (in Giles, Gems of Chinese Literature)

speaker: samuel-johnson
text: Is not a Patron, my Lord, one who looks with unconcern on a man struggling for life in the water, and, when he has reached ground, encumbers him with help?
work: Letter to Lord Chesterfield, February 1755
note: as printed in Boswell's Life of Johnson

speaker: sophocles
text: Nor did I deem that thou, a mortal man, Could’st by a breath annul and override The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven. They were not born today nor yesterday; They die not; and none knoweth whence they sprang.
work: Antigone
note: spoken by Antigone to King Creon

speaker: ibn-tufayl
text: …like the Image of the Sun which appears in a well-polish'd Looking-glass, which is neither the Sun nor the Looking-glass, and yet not distinct from them.
work: Hayy ibn Yaqzan, section 90
note: of what his hero Hayy beheld in contemplation

speaker: gustave-flaubert
text: We must not touch our idols; the gilt sticks to our fingers.
work: Madame Bovary (1857), part 3

speaker: jane-austen
text: All the privilege I claim for my own sex (it is not a very enviable one; you need not covet it), is that of loving longest, when existence or when hope is gone.
work: Persuasion (1817), chapter 23
note: spoken by Anne Elliot

speaker: william-blake
text: In every cry of every man, In every infant's cry of fear, In every voice, in every ban, The mind-forged manacles I hear…
work: London, Songs of Experience (1794)

speaker: aeschylus
text: On, sons of Greece! On, for your country’s freedom! strike to save Wives, children, temples of ancestral gods, Graves of your fathers! now is all at stake.
work: The Persians
note: the Greek battle cry at Salamis, as a Persian messenger reports it in the play

speaker: jami
text: O Lord, none but Thyself can fathom Thee, Yet every mosque and church doth harbour Thee; I know the seekers and what 'tis they seek— Seekers and sought are all comprised in Thee.
work: Lawa'ih (Flashes of Light)
credit: tr. E. H. Whinfield, 1906 (in F. Hadland Davis, The Persian Mystics: Jami, 1908)

speaker: sigmund-freud
text: To bear life remains, after all, the first duty of the living.
work: Thoughts for the Times on War and Death (1915)
credit: tr. A. A. Brill and Alfred B. Kuttner, 1918

speaker: william-wordsworth
text: I wandered lonely as a Cloud That floats on high o'er Vales and Hills, When all at once I saw a crowd A host of dancing Daffodills; Along the Lake, beneath the trees, Ten thousand dancing in the breeze.
work: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud, Poems in Two Volumes (1807)

speaker: johann-wolfgang-von-goethe
text: I am the Spirit that Denies! And justly so: for all things, from the Void Called forth, deserve to be destroyed…
work: Faust, part 1 (1808), the Study
note: spoken by Mephistopheles

speaker: euripides
text: What else is Wisdom? What of man's endeavour Or God's high grace, so lovely and so great? To stand from fear set free, to breathe and wait; To hold a hand uplifted over Hate; And shall not Loveliness be loved for ever?
work: The Bacchae
note: sung by the chorus

speaker: theodor-herzl
text: We shall live at last as free men on our own soil, and die peacefully in our own homes.
work: The Jewish State (1896), conclusion
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: geoffrey-of-monmouth
text: …offered me a very ancient book in the British tongue, which, in a continued regular story and elegant style, related the actions of them all, from Brutus the first king of the Britons, down to Cadwallader the son of Cadwallo.
work: History of the Kings of Britain, book 1, dedication
credit: tr. Aaron Thompson, rev. J. A. Giles, 1848
note: the book no one else ever saw, his claimed source
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: friedrich-schiller
text: But the strong man is the strongest when alone.
work: Wilhelm Tell (1804), act 1, scene 3
note: spoken by Tell

speaker: pindar
text: Best is Water of all, and Gold as a flaming fire in the night shineth eminent amid lordly wealth…
work: Olympian Odes, 1

speaker: ludwig-van-beethoven
text: Like the State, each man must have his own constitution.
work: Diary, 1815

speaker: jose-rizal
text: …since we mortals in general are very much like tortoises: we are esteemed and classified according to our shells…
work: The Social Cancer (Noli Me Tangere, 1887), ch. 2

speaker: shinran
text: Difficult is it for men to find a wise Teacher; so is it also for them to be instructed and to hear the Holy Law. More difficult still is it to receive the True Faith.
work: Wasan (hymns), 67
credit: tr. S. Yamabe and L. Adams Beck, 1921

speaker: wolfgang-amadeus-mozart
text: I am a composer, and born to become a Kapellmeister, and I neither can nor ought thus to bury the talent for composition with which God has so richly endowed me…
work: Letter to his father, Mannheim, 7 February 1778

speaker: solon
text: Each day grow older, and learn something new…
work: a line of his verse, quoted in Plutarch's Life of Solon
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859

speaker: cesare-beccaria
text: We shall see, if we open histories, that laws, which are or ought to be covenants between free men, have generally been nothing but the instrument of the passions of some few men, or the result of some accidental and temporary necessity.
work: On Crimes and Punishments (1764), introduction

speaker: lajos-kossuth
text: My beloved native land! thy very sufferings make thee but dearer to my heart; thy bleeding image dwells with me when I wake, as it rests with me in the short moments of my restless sleep.
work: Speech on his welcome to New York, December 1851
note: spoken in English, in exile after the Hungarian revolution
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: prince-shotoku
text: Their right is our wrong, and our right is their wrong. We are not unquestionably sages, nor are they unquestionably fools. Both of us are simply ordinary men.
work: Seventeen-Article Constitution, 604, article 10 (Nihongi, book 22)
note: the constitution the Nihongi attributes to him
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: sappho
text: As the sweet-apple blushes on the end of the bough, the very end of the bough, which the gatherers overlooked, nay overlooked not but could not reach.
work: Fragments

speaker: moliere
text: Nature, when we leave her free, will herself gently recover from the disorder into which she has fallen. It is our anxiety, our impatience, which does the mischief, and most men die of their remedies, and not of their diseases.
work: The Imaginary Invalid (1673), act 3
note: spoken by Béralde

speaker: aristophanes
text: …old men are boys twice over, and that it is the more reasonable that the old should weep than the young, inasmuch as it is less just that they should err.
work: The Clouds
note: spoken by Pheidippides, defending his right to beat his father

speaker: charlemagne
text: …those who desire to please God by living rightly should not neglect to please him also by speaking correctly.
work: Letter to Abbot Baugulf of Fulda (On the Cultivation of Letters)
note: a letter issued in his name, probably drafted by Alcuin

speaker: grover-cleveland
text: …the lesson should be constantly enforced that, though the people support the government, the government should not support the people.
work: Veto of the Texas seed bill, 16 February 1887
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: jean-racine
text: No longer is it love hid in my heart, But Venus in her might seizing her prey.
work: Phaedra (1677), act 1, scene 3
note: spoken by Phaedra

speaker: james-cook
text: From what I have said of the Natives of New Holland they may appear to some to be the most wretched People upon Earth; but in reality they are far more happier than we Europeans…
work: Journal of the first voyage, August 1770

speaker: xenophon
text: We have had occasion before now to reflect how often democracies have been overthrown by the desire for some other type of government, how often monarchies and oligarchies have been swept away by movements of the people…
work: Cyropaedia, book 1

speaker: ibn-arabi
text: Every one praises what he believes; his god is his own creature, and in praising it he praises himself.
work: On creeds (in Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam)

speaker: george-eliot
text: If we had a keen vision and feeling of all ordinary human life, it would be like hearing the grass grow and the squirrel’s heart beat, and we should die of that roar which lies on the other side of silence.
work: Middlemarch (1872), ch. 20

speaker: samuel-pepys
text: The churches, houses, and all on fire and flaming at once; and a horrid noise the flames made, and the cracking of houses at their ruins.
work: Diary, 2 September 1666, the Great Fire of London

speaker: daniel-defoe
text: Wherever God erects a house of prayer, The Devil always builds a chapel there: And 'twill be found upon examination, The latter has the largest congregation…
work: The True-Born Englishman (1701), part 1

speaker: plutarch
text: Reputation is like flame. There is no difficulty in keeping it alive; it merely requires a little feeding with fuel. But let either of them become extinct and cold, and it will take some trouble to rekindle.
work: On Old Men in Public Life (Moralia)

speaker: pope-gregory-i
text: For things are not to be loved for the sake of places, but places for the sake of good things.
work: Answers to Augustine of Canterbury (Bede, Ecclesiastical History, book 1, chapter 27)
note: his answer to Augustine of Canterbury on the customs of the Churches, preserved by Bede

speaker: william-mckinley
text: Lynchings must not be tolerated in a great and civilized country like the United States; courts, not mobs, must execute the penalties of the law.
work: First Inaugural Address (1897)

speaker: henry-fielding
text: …love may again be likened to a disease in this, that when it is denied a vent in one part, it will certainly break out in another.
work: Tom Jones (1749), book 4, chapter 12

speaker: alexander-von-humboldt
text: In the solitude of the seas we hail a star as a friend, from whom we have long been separated.
work: Personal Narrative, chapter 2

speaker: pompey
text: …whenever I stamp with my foot in any part of Italy, there will rise up forces enough in an instant, both horse and foot.
work: Plutarch, Life of Pompey
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to those who asked what forces could stop Caesar, 50 BCE

speaker: einhard
text: He tried also to learn to write, and for this purpose used to carry with him and keep under the pillow of his couch tablets and writing-sheets that he might in his spare moments accustom himself to the formation of letters.
work: Life of Charlemagne, chapter 25

speaker: pierre-joseph-proudhon
text: Although a firm friend of order, I am (in the full force of the term) an anarchist.
work: What Is Property? (1840), ch. 5

speaker: oliver-goldsmith
text: While words of learned length, and thundering sound, Amazed the gazing rustics ranged around; And still they gazed, and still the wonder grew That one small head could carry all he knew.
work: The Deserted Village (1770), the village schoolmaster

speaker: george-berkeley
text: …the far greater part, if not all, of those difficulties which have hitherto amused philosophers, and blocked up the way to knowledge, are entirely owing to ourselves--that we have first raised a dust and then complain we cannot see.
work: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710), introduction

speaker: sallust
text: Accordingly, good morals were cultivated at home and in the field; there was the greatest harmony and little or no avarice; justice and probity prevailed among them, thanks not so much to laws as to nature.
work: The War with Catiline, 9
note: of the early Roman Republic

speaker: gregory-of-tours
text: …although my speech is rude, I have been unable to be silent as to the struggles between the wicked and the upright…
work: History of the Franks, first preface

speaker: mahatma-gandhi
text: Civilization is that mode of conduct which points out to man the path of duty. Performance of duty and observance of morality are convertible terms.
work: Hind Swaraj (Indian Home Rule), ch. 13 (1909)
note: spoken by the Editor in the dialogue

speaker: qianlong-emperor
text: As your Ambassador can see for himself, we possess all things. I set no value on objects strange or ingenious, and have no use for your country's manufactures.
work: Edict to King George III, 1793
credit: tr. E. Backhouse and J. O. P. Bland, 1914

speaker: jeremy-bentham
text: They govern us in all we do, in all we say, in all we think: every effort we can make to throw off our subjection, will serve but to demonstrate and confirm it.
work: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789), chapter 1
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: kalidasa
text: The good who hear me will be glad To pluck the good from out the bad; When ore is proved by fire, the loss Is not of purest gold, but dross.
work: The Dynasty of Raghu, canto 1

speaker: pope-urban-ii
text: When an armed attack is made upon the enemy, let this one cry be raised by all the soldiers of God: It is the will of God! It is the will of God!
work: Speech at the Council of Clermont, 1095 (Robert the Monk's version)
note: the speech as Robert the Monk, who was there, retold it some years later

speaker: albert-einstein
text: No fairer destiny could be allotted to any physical theory, than that it should of itself point out the way to the introduction of a more comprehensive theory, in which it lives on as a limiting case.
work: Relativity: The Special and General Theory (1916), ch. 22

speaker: gottfried-wilhelm-leibniz
text: Each portion of matter may be conceived as like a garden full of plants and like a pond full of fishes. But each branch of every plant, each member of every animal, each drop of its liquid parts is also some such garden or pond.
work: The Monadology (1714), section 67
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: red-jacket
text: You say there is but one way to worship and serve the Great Spirit. If there is but one religion, why do you white people differ so much about it? Why not all agreed, as you can all read the book?
work: Reply to the missionary Jacob Cram, Buffalo Creek, 1805
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: gaius-marius
text: For my part, I believe that all men have one and the same nature, but that the bravest is the best born…
work: Speech to the Roman people (Sallust, The Jugurthine War, 85)
note: Sallust's version of his speech on being elected consul, 107 BCE

speaker: mikhail-bakunin
text: In the matter of boots, I refer to the authority of the bootmaker; concerning houses, canals, or railroads, I consult that of the architect or engineer.
work: God and the State (written 1871)

speaker: alfred-the-great
text: In this we can still see their tracks, but we cannot follow them, and therefore we have lost both the wealth and the wisdom, because we would not incline our hearts after their example.
work: Preface to the Pastoral Care
note: the words he imagines the old places of learning saying of their forefathers
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: gotthold-ephraim-lessing
text: How can I less believe in my forefathers Than thou in thine. How can I ask of thee To own that thy forefathers falsified In order to yield mine the praise of truth.
work: Nathan the Wise (1779), act 3, scene 7
note: spoken by Nathan to Saladin

speaker: william-bligh
text: I now unhappily saw that nothing could be done to effect the recovery of the ship: there was no one to assist me, and every endeavour on my part was answered with threats of death.
work: A Narrative of the Mutiny on Board His Majesty's Ship Bounty (1790), 28 April 1789

speaker: marcus-aurelius
text: …for the mind converts and changes every hindrance to its activity into an aid; and so that which is a hindrance is made a furtherance to an act; and that which is an obstacle on the road helps us on this road.
work: Meditations, book 5

speaker: louis-ix-of-france
text: For there is no leprosy so foul as deadly sin, seeing that a soul in deadly sin is in the image of the Devil.
work: Words to Joinville (Joinville, Memoirs)
note: as Jean de Joinville recorded them

speaker: peter-kropotkin
text: …those species which best know how to combine, and to avoid competition, have the best chances of survival and of a further progressive development. They prosper, while the unsociable species decay.
work: Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution (1902), ch. 3

speaker: theobald-wolfe-tone
text: Under the flag of the French Republic I originally engaged with a view to save and liberate my own country.
work: Speech to his court martial, Dublin, 10 November 1798
note: as recorded in Speeches from the Dock (1867)

speaker: william-wilberforce
text: We profess a religion which inculcates truth and love, peace and good-will, among men—We are foremost in a commerce which exists but by war, treachery, and devastation.
work: A Letter on the Abolition of the Slave Trade (1807)

speaker: boethius
text: Love, all-sovereign Love!—oh, then, Ye are blest, ye sons of men, If the love that rules the sky In your hearts is throned on high!
work: The Consolation of Philosophy, book 2
note: sung by Philosophy, who visits him in prison

speaker: john-stuart-mill
text: It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.
work: Utilitarianism (1863), ch. 2

speaker: thomas-more
text: I am persuaded that till property is taken away, there can be no equitable or just distribution of things, nor can the world be happily governed…
work: Utopia, book 1
note: spoken by the traveller Raphael Hythloday in the dialogue

speaker: leo-tolstoy
text: …the hero of my tale, the one I love with all the power of my soul, the one I have tried to reproduce in all his beauty, just as he has been, is, and always will be beautiful, is Truth.
work: Sevastopol in May (1855), closing words

speaker: franklin-d-roosevelt
text: We have learned that we cannot live alone, at peace; that our own well-being is dependent on the well-being of other nations far away. We have learned that we must live as men, not as ostriches, nor as dogs in the manger.
work: Fourth Inaugural Address (1945)

speaker: pyrrhus-of-epirus
text: …it is impossible for any man to avoid his fate; but neither he nor any other Italian shall have much satisfaction in engaging with me.
work: Plutarch, Life of Pyrrhus
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to an officer warning him of an Italian horseman, at Heraclea

speaker: tecumseh
text: We must compare our father's conduct to a fat dog, that carries its tail upon its back, but when affrighted, it drops it between its legs and runs off.
work: Speech to General Procter, Amherstburg, September 1813
note: text as printed in B. B. Thatcher, Indian Biography (1832)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: giovanni-boccaccio
text: …vast trenches, wherein those who came after were laid by the hundred and being heaped up therein by layers, as goods are stowed aboard ship, were covered with a little earth, till such time as they reached the top of the trench.
work: The Decameron, day 1, introduction (the plague in Florence, 1348)

speaker: friedrich-engels
text: The English working-men call this “social murder,” and accuse our whole society of perpetrating this crime perpetually. Are they wrong?
work: The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845)

speaker: woodrow-wilson
text: We are provincials no longer. The tragic events of the thirty months of vital turmoil through which we have just passed have made us citizens of the world. There can be no turning back.
work: Second Inaugural Address (1917)

speaker: thomas-paine
text: Independence is my happiness, and I view things as they are, without regard to place or person; my country is the world, and my religion is to do good.
work: Rights of Man, part 2, chapter 5 (1792)

speaker: marcus-furius-camillus
text: There are laws of war as well of peace; and we have learned to wage them justly not less than bravely. We carry arms not against that age which is spared even when towns are taken, but against men who are themselves armed…
work: Livy, History of Rome, book 5
note: to the schoolmaster of Falerii, who had brought him the children of the town as hostages

speaker: michelangelo
text: Now hath my life across a stormy sea Like a frail bark reached that wide port where all Are bidden, ere the final reckoning fall Of good and evil for eternity.
work: Sonnet 65, to Giorgio Vasari, on the brink of death

speaker: livy
text: This indulgence is conceded to antiquity, that by blending things human with divine, it may make the origin of cities appear more venerable…
work: History of Rome, preface
note: on the legends of Rome's founding

speaker: jahangir
text: …although I myself drink wine, and from the age of 18 years up till now, when I am 38, have persisted in it.
work: Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (his memoirs), his edict against making wine
credit: tr. Alexander Rogers, ed. Henry Beveridge, 1909

speaker: rabindranath-tagore
text: The same stream of life that runs through my veins night and day runs through the world and dances in rhythmic measures.
work: Gitanjali, 69 (1912)

speaker: pliny-the-younger
text: But faithful friends are so rare, and the dead so soon forgotten, that we shall be obliged ourselves to build even our very tombs, and anticipate the office of our heirs.
work: Letters, book 6, letter 10
credit: tr. William Melmoth, rev. F. C. T. Bosanquet, 1915
note: on the unfinished tomb of the general Verginius Rufus

speaker: albrecht-durer
text: …all the days of my life I have seen nothing that reaches my heart so much as these, for among them I have seen wonderfully artistic things and have admired the subtle ingenuity of men in foreign lands…
work: Diary of the journey to the Netherlands, 1520, on the Aztec treasures sent to Charles V

speaker: abul-fazl-ibn-mubarak
text: I longed for interviews with the Llámas of Tibet or with the pádris of Portugal, and I would gladly sit with the priests of the Pársís and the learned of the Zend-ávestá.
work: On his youth, before he came to Akbar's court
credit: English translation quoted by G. B. Malleson, 1890

speaker: swami-vivekananda
text: Come up, O lions, and shake off the delusion that you are sheep; you are souls immortal, spirits free, blest and eternal…
work: Paper on Hinduism, Parliament of Religions, Chicago, 1893
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: james-madison
text: It could never be more truly said than of the first remedy, that it was worse than the disease. Liberty is to faction what air is to fire, an aliment without which it instantly expires.
work: The Federalist No. 10 (1787)
note: published under the name Publius

speaker: trajan
text: Anonymous informations ought not to be received in any sort of prosecution. It is introducing a very dangerous precedent, and is quite foreign to the spirit of our age.
work: Letter to Pliny the Younger (Pliny, Letters, book 10, letter 97)
credit: tr. William Melmoth, rev. F. C. T. Bosanquet, 1915
note: his reply on the Christians of Bithynia

speaker: bernal-diaz-del-castillo
text: If I were desirous of relating every circumstance I should never finish, and my book would resemble 'Amadis de Gaule,' and other such romances, whose authors can find no end to their pretty stories.
work: The True History of the Conquest of New Spain (the siege of Tenochtitlan)

speaker: theodore-roosevelt
text: The conservation of our natural resources and their proper use constitute the fundamental problem which underlies almost every other problem of our National life.
work: Annual message to Congress (1907)

speaker: giorgio-vasari
text: …in learning and in the rudiments of letters he would have made great proficience, if he had not been so variable and unstable, for he set himself to learn many things, and then, after having begun them, abandoned them.
work: Lives of the Artists, Leonardo da Vinci
credit: tr. Gaston du C. de Vere, 1912

speaker: david-livingstone
text: The mere animal pleasure of travelling in a wild unexplored country is very great.
work: Journal, 26 March 1866 (The Last Journals, 1874)

speaker: lucretius
text: Whilst human kind Throughout the lands lay miserably crushed Before all eyes beneath Religion—who Would show her head along the region skies, Glowering on mortals with her hideous face…
work: On the Nature of Things, book 1
note: of Epicurus, the Greek who first stood up to religion

speaker: william-caxton
text: And certainly our language now used varieth far from that which was used and spoken when I was born.
work: Prologue to the Eneydos (1490)

speaker: teresa-of-avila
text: I saw in his hand a long spear of gold, and at the iron's point there seemed to be a little fire.
work: The Life of St. Teresa, chapter 29 (the vision of the angel)

speaker: b-r-ambedkar
text: …class and caste, so to say, are next door neighbours, and it is only a span that separates the two. A caste is an enclosed class.
work: Castes in India: Their Mechanism, Genesis and Development (1917)
note: a paper read at Columbia University, 1916

speaker: akbar
text: I cannot bear that any misunderstanding should subsist between you and those who have for so many years shared in my toils, and been the companions of my glory.
work: On his deathbed, 1605
credit: English translation quoted by G. B. Malleson, 1890
note: asking that his nobles be summoned to him

speaker: catullus
text: I hate and I love. Wherefore do I so, peradventure thou askest. I know not, but I feel it to be thus and I suffer.
work: Poems, 85

speaker: georgius-agricola
text: And when the woods and groves are felled, then are exterminated the beasts and birds, very many of which furnish a pleasant and agreeable food for man.
work: De Re Metallica (1556), book 1
credit: tr. Herbert Clark Hoover and Lou Henry Hoover, 1912
note: the critics' case against mining, which he sets out before answering it

speaker: muhammad-iqbal
text: That which fortifies personality is good, that which weakens it is bad.
work: Statement of his philosophy, in R. A. Nicholson's introduction to The Secrets of the Self (1920)
note: written for his translator, who gave it "in his own words as nearly as possible"

speaker: olaudah-equiano
text: I who had been a slave in the morning, trembling at the will of another, was become my own master, and completely free.
work: The Interesting Narrative (1789), chapter 7, on buying his freedom in 1766

speaker: louis-pasteur
text: They are the temples of the future, of riches and of comfort. There humanity grows greater, better, stronger; there she can learn to read the works of Nature, works of progress and universal harmony…
work: Le Budget de la science (1868), on laboratories
note: quoted in René Vallery-Radot's Life of Pasteur

speaker: terence
text: Quarrels of lovers but renew their love.
work: The Woman of Andros, act 3

speaker: alvar-nunez-cabeza-de-vaca
text: …sat down among us, and from the sorrow and pity they felt, they all began to lament so earnestly that they might have been heard at a distance, and continued so doing more than half an hour.
work: Relation (1542), chapter 12 (the shipwreck on the Texas coast, 1528)

speaker: christopher-marlowe
text: Hell hath no limits, nor is circumscrib'd In one self-place; but where we are is hell, And where hell is, there must we ever be…
work: Doctor Faustus, act 2
note: spoken by the devil Mephistophilis

speaker: ben-jonson
text: Triumph, my Britain, thou hast one to show, To whom all scenes of Europe homage owe. He was not of an age, but for all time!
work: To the Memory of My Beloved, the Author, Mr William Shakespeare (1623)

speaker: aesop
text: Slow but steady wins the race.
work: The Hare and the Tortoise
note: the fable's moral, as Townsend's collection gives it

speaker: camillo-benso-count-of-cavour
text: Having little artistic taste, I feel sure that in the midst of the splendid monuments of ancient and modern Rome I shall lament the plain and unpoetic streets of my native town.
work: Speech to the Italian parliament on Rome as the capital, 1861
credit: tr. in The World's Famous Orations, ed. William Jennings Bryan, 1906 (translator not named)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: anselm-of-canterbury
text: And indeed, we believe that you are a being than which nothing greater can be conceived.
work: Proslogion, chapter 2

speaker: tertullian
text: What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What concord is there between the Academy and the Church? what between heretics and Christians?
work: The Prescription against Heretics, 7

speaker: walter-raleigh
text: …a sharp medicine, but one that will cure me of all my diseases.
work: Words on the scaffold, 29 October 1618, touching the axe
note: as reported by the witnesses, in Edmund Gosse's life of him (1886)

speaker: croesus
text: Alas! my own sufferings, by their very bitterness, have taught me to be keen-sighted of dangers.
work: Herodotus, Histories, book 1 (counsel to Cyrus before the war with the Massagetae)
note: Herodotus's account
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: helmuth-von-moltke-the-elder
text: Every law necessitates an authority to watch over it and to direct its execution, but there is no power which can enforce obedience to international agreements.
work: Letter to Johann Kaspar Bluntschli on the laws of war, 1880

speaker: dante-alighieri
text: Consider ye the seed from which ye sprang; Ye were not made to live like unto brutes, But for pursuit of virtue and of knowledge.
work: Divine Comedy, Inferno, canto 26
note: spoken by Ulysses, urging his crew on to the unknown

speaker: torquato-tasso
text: So we, if children young diseased we find, Anoint with sweets the vessel’s foremost parts To make them taste the potions sharp we give; They drink deceived, and so deceived, they live.
work: Jerusalem Delivered, canto 1

speaker: frederick-the-great
text: I am in the case of a traveller who sees himself surrounded and ready to be assassinated by a troop of cut-throats, who intend to share his spoils.
work: Letter to his sister Wilhelmine, July 1757

speaker: darius-i
text: …where it is necessary that a lie be spoken, let it be spoken; seeing that we all aim at the same object, both they who lie and they who always speak the truth…
work: Herodotus, Histories, book 3 (to Otanes, before the attack on the Magi)

work: Plutarch, Life of Cato the Younger
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to one who told him that men blamed his silence

speaker: chongzhen-emperor
text: I am ashamed to meet my ancestors; and therefore I myself take off my crown, and with my hair covering my face, await dismemberment at the hands of the rebels. Do not hurt a single one of my people!
work: His last decree, written as Beijing fell, 1644 (in Giles, Gems of Chinese Literature)

speaker: henry-viii-of-england
text: …methinketh the time longer since your departing now last, than I was wont to do a whole fortnight.
work: Letter to Anne Boleyn, 1528

speaker: ulysses-s-grant
text: For myself, I was bitterly opposed to the measure, and to this day regard the war, which resulted, as one of the most unjust ever waged by a stronger against a weaker nation.
work: Personal Memoirs (1885), on the war with Mexico

speaker: boudica
text: If you weigh well the strength of the armies, and the causes of the war, you will see that in this battle you must conquer or die. This is a woman's resolve; as for men, they may live and be slaves.
work: Speech to the Britons before battle (Tacitus, Annals, book 14)
credit: tr. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb, 1876
note: Tacitus's version of her words from her chariot, 60 or 61 CE

speaker: lajos-kossuth
text: I have no idea but thee; I have no feeling but thee.
work: Speech on his welcome to New York, December 1851
note: spoken in English, of his homeland
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: snorri-sturluson
text: As to funeral rites, the earliest age is called the Age of Burning; because all the dead were consumed by fire, and over their ashes were raised standing stones.
work: Heimskringla, preface

speaker: hugo-grotius
text: Thus two and two must make four, nor is it possible to be otherwise; nor, again, can what is really evil not be evil.
work: On the Law of War and Peace (1625), book 1, chapter 1

speaker: tiberius
text: These sentiments of your hearts are my temples, these my most glorious and abiding monuments. Those built of stone are despised as mere tombs, if the judgment of posterity passes into hatred.
work: Speech to the Senate, 25 CE (Tacitus, Annals, book 4)
credit: tr. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb, 1876
note: refusing a temple to himself, as Tacitus gives it

speaker: claudius
text: Are we sorry that the Balbi came to us from Spain, and other men not less illustrious from Narbon Gaul? Their descendants are still among us, and do not yield to us in patriotism.
work: Speech to the Senate on admitting Gauls, 48 CE (Tacitus, Annals, book 11)
credit: tr. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb, 1876
note: Tacitus's version of the speech

speaker: charles-stewart-parnell
text: One alternative is the coercion which Lord Salisbury put before the country, and the other is the alternative offered by the prime minister, carrying with it the lasting settlement of a treaty of peace.
work: Speech on the Home Rule Bill, House of Commons, 1886
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: harold-godwinson
text: …will give him seven feet of English ground, or as much more as he may be taller than other men.
work: His offer to Harald Hardrada before Stamford Bridge, 1066 (Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla)
note: spoken by Harold himself, riding up unrecognised among the horsemen, in Snorri's saga written about 1230

speaker: alphonse-de-lamartine
text: Poland is dear to us; Italy is dear to us; all oppressed peoples are dear to us; but France to us is dearer than all…
work: Reply to a deputation of Polish exiles, 1848
credit: tr. in The World's Famous Orations, ed. William Jennings Bryan, 1906 (translator not named)
note: spoken as foreign minister of the French Republic
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: germanicus
text: It is not the chief duty of friends to follow the dead with unprofitable laments, but to remember his wishes, to fulfil his commands.
work: Tacitus, Annals, book 2
credit: tr. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb, 1876
note: his words to his friends as he lay dying at Antioch, 19 CE, as Tacitus gives them

speaker: grover-cleveland
text: Federal aid in such cases encourages the expectation of paternal care on the part of the government and weakens the sturdiness of our national character…
work: Veto of the Texas seed bill, 16 February 1887
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: protagoras
text: Concerning the Gods, I am not able to know to a certainty whether they exist or whether they do not. For there are many things which prevent one from knowing, especially the obscurity of the subject, and the shortness of the life of man.
work: On the Gods, opening (Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 9)
note: the treatise for which, Diogenes says, the Athenians banished him and burnt his books

speaker: harald-hardrada
text: …and they who stand in the first rank shall set the spear-shaft on the ground, and the spear-point against the horseman's breast, if he rides at them; and those who stand in the second rank shall set the spear-point against the horse's breast.
work: Orders to his army at Stamford Bridge, 1066 (Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla)
note: Snorri's saga, written about 1230

speaker: john-adams
text: It ought to be solemnized with pomp and parade, with shows, games, sports, guns, bells, bonfires, and illuminations, from one end of this continent to the other, from this time forward forevermore.
work: Letter to Abigail Adams on the vote for independence, 3 July 1776

speaker: sun-yat-sen
text: In a nutshell, it is my idea to make capitalism create socialism in China so that these two economic forces of human evolution will work side by side in future civilization.
work: The International Development of China (1922), conclusion

speaker: william-mckinley
text: We want no wars of conquest; we must avoid the temptation of territorial aggression. War should never be entered upon until every agency of peace has failed; peace is preferable to war in almost every contingency.
work: First Inaugural Address (1897)

speaker: pliny-the-elder
text: For all over the world, in all places, and at all times, Fortune is the only god whom every one invokes; she alone is spoken of, she alone is accused and is supposed to be guilty…
work: Natural History, book 2
credit: tr. John Bostock and H. T. Riley, 1855

speaker: james-monroe
text: …the American continents, by the free and independent condition which they have assumed and maintain, are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers.
work: Annual message to Congress (the Monroe Doctrine), 1823

speaker: gelimer
text: But as for me, I am not able to write further. For my present misfortune has robbed me of my thoughts. Farewell, then, dear Pharas, and send me a lyre and one loaf of bread and a sponge, I pray you.
work: Letter from the siege on Mount Papua, 533-534 (Procopius, History of the Wars, book 4)
note: the last Vandal king's answer to the besieging commander Pharas, as Procopius gives it

speaker: ferdinand-lassalle
text: …in a morally adjusted community there must be added to it solidarity of interests, mutual consideration, and mutual helpfulness in development.
work: The Workingmen's Programme, lecture in Berlin, 1862

speaker: augustine-of-hippo
text: What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not…
work: Confessions, book 11

speaker: otto-von-bismarck
text: We Germans had no longer any reason for war. We had what we needed. To fight for more, from a lust of conquest and for the annexation of countries which were not necessary for us, always appeared to me like an atrocity…
work: Speech to students on his eightieth birthday, Friedrichsruh, 1 April 1895

speaker: andrew-jackson
text: It is to be regretted that the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to their selfish purposes. Distinctions in society will always exist under every just government.
work: Veto message on the Bank of the United States, 1832

speaker: aethelberht-of-kent
text: Your words and promises are fair, but because they are new to us, and of uncertain import, I cannot consent to them so far as to forsake that which I have so long observed with the whole English nation.
work: Answer to Augustine of Canterbury, 597 (Bede, Ecclesiastical History, book 1, chapter 25)
note: Bede's account

speaker: tacitus
text: Indeed never has it been proved by such terrible disasters to Rome or by such clear evidence that Providence is concerned not with our peace of mind but rather with vengeance for our sin.
work: Histories, book 1
note: of the year of the four emperors and the civil wars that followed

speaker: john-stuart-mill
text: That the principle which regulates the existing social relations between the two sexes—the legal subordination of one sex to the other—is wrong in itself, and now one of the chief hindrances to human improvement…
work: The Subjection of Women (1869), ch. 1

speaker: thomas-paine
text: The summer soldier and the sunshine patriot will, in this crisis, shrink from the service of their country; but he that stands it now, deserves the love and thanks of man and woman.
work: The American Crisis, no. 1 (December 1776)

speaker: amos-prophet
text: But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
work: Amos 5:24
note: the prophet speaking in the name of God
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: olaf-ii-of-norway
text: When we come into battle we shall all have one countersign and field-cry,—'Forward, forward, Christian men! cross men! king's men!
work: Speech to his army before Stiklestad, 1030 (Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla)
note: Snorri's saga, written about 1230

speaker: friedrich-engels
text: The first class antagonism appearing in history coincides with the development of the antagonism of man and wife in monogamy, and the first class oppression with that of the female by the male sex.
work: The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State (1884), ch. 2

speaker: james-madison
text: Justice is the end of government. It is the end of civil society. It ever has been and ever will be pursued until it be obtained, or until liberty be lost in the pursuit.
work: The Federalist No. 51 (1788)
note: published under the name Publius

speaker: nehemiah
text: Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.
work: Nehemiah 2:17, to the people of Jerusalem
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: george-washington-williams
text: By such means as these, too silly and disgusting to mention, and a few boxes of gin, whole villages have been signed away to your Majesty.
work: Open letter to King Leopold II on the Congo, 1890
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: averroes
text: …a man who prevents another fit for it, from studying the books of philosophy, because certain worthless people have been misled by them, is like a man who refused a thirsty man cold and sweet water, till he died…
work: The Decisive Treatise (Fasl al-Maqal)

speaker: kabir
text: O servant, where dost thou seek Me? Lo! I am beside thee. I am neither in temple nor in mosque: I am neither in Kaaba nor in Kailash…
work: Songs of Kabir, I
note: the voice is God's, speaking in the poem

speaker: ramesses-iii
text: I caused the whole country to be planted with groves of trees and with flowering shrubs, and I made the people to sit under the shade thereof.
work: Great Harris Papyrus, summary of his reign
note: the account of his reign written in his name in the Great Harris Papyrus, completed after his death

speaker: jose-de-san-martin
text: Until now the United Provinces have fought for no one knows what, without a flag, and without any avowed principles to explain the origin and tendency of the insurrection. We must declare ourselves independent if we wish to be known and respected.
work: Spoken among friends in Buenos Aires, c. 1812
note: as quoted in Bartolomé Mitre's history, The Emancipation of South America

speaker: bartolome-mitre
text: Time, which dissipates false and enhances true glory, has thrown much light upon matters which during their lifetime seemed obscure.
work: The Emancipation of South America (history of San Martín)

speaker: thomas-aquinas
text: Thus to every taste the sweet is pleasant but to some, the sweetness of wine is most pleasant, to others, the sweetness of honey, or of something similar.
work: Summa Theologica, part 1-2, question 1, article 7
credit: tr. Fathers of the English Dominican Province, 1920

speaker: julius-caesar
text: I have not just cause to weep, when I consider that Alexander at my age had conquered so many nations, and I have all this time done nothing that is memorable?
work: Plutarch, Life of Caesar
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to his friends in Spain, who found him in tears after reading the history of Alexander

speaker: alexander-the-great
text: This, it seems, is royalty.
work: Plutarch, Life of Alexander
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: on entering the luxurious tent of the Persian king Darius III, captured after Issus

speaker: olaudah-equiano
text: We are almost a nation of dancers, musicians, and poets.
work: The Interesting Narrative (1789), on the Igbo country of his childhood

speaker: herbert-spencer
text: How to live?—that is the essential question for us. Not how to live in the mere material sense only, but in the widest sense.
work: What Knowledge Is of Most Worth? (1859), in Essays on Education

speaker: hernan-cortes
text: …you knowe, that when I came into thys Countrey, I commaunded all my Shippes to be sonke, so that nowe I haue néede of time conueniente to builde vessels to carrie vs into oure Countrey…
work: To Moctezuma, 1520 (Gómara's history)
note: reported by Francisco López de Gómara, his chaplain and biographer

speaker: cicero
text: You might just as well take the sun out of the sky as friendship from life; for the immortal gods have given us nothing better or more delightful.
work: On Friendship
note: Gaius Laelius is the speaker in the dialogue

speaker: james-vi-and-i
text: …the husband shall not bee ashamed, to reduce thereby his delicate, wholesome, and cleane complexioned wife, to that extremetie, that either shee must also corrupt her sweete breath therewith, or else resolue to liue in a perpetuall stinking torment.
work: A Counterblaste to Tobacco (1604)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: cao-cao
text: Better to jilt than be jilted: better to sin than to be sinned against.
work: A saying (in Giles, Gems of Chinese Literature)
note: Giles gives it as his famous saying

speaker: millicent-garrett-fawcett
text: If the nineteenth century was a time of education for women, it was no less a time of education for men.
work: Women's Suffrage: A Short History of a Great Movement (1912)

speaker: maimonides
text: …when I find the road narrow, and can see no other way of teaching a well established truth except by pleasing one intelligent man and displeasing ten thousand fools—I prefer to address myself to the one man…
work: The Guide for the Perplexed, introduction

speaker: ovid
text: The Golden Age was first founded, which, without any avenger, of its own accord, without laws, practised both faith and rectitude.
work: Metamorphoses, book 1

speaker: diogenes-the-cynic
text: …be an absurd thing if Agesilaus and Epaminondas are to live in the mud, and some miserable wretches, who have been initiated, are to be in the islands of the blest.
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 6
note: his reply to the Athenians who urged him to be initiated into the Mysteries, which promised the initiated the best places after death

speaker: michael-faraday
text: …that you may, like it, shine as lights to those about you; that, in all your actions, you may justify the beauty of the taper by making your deeds honourable and effectual in the discharge of your duty to your fellow-men.
work: The Chemical History of a Candle (1861), closing words
note: Christmas lectures for young people at the Royal Institution

speaker: justus-von-liebig
text: The quantity of soap consumed by a nation would be no inaccurate measure whereby to estimate its wealth and civilisation. Of two countries, with an equal amount of population, the wealthiest and most highly civilised will consume the greatest weight of soap.
work: Familiar Letters on Chemistry (1843), letter 2

speaker: marco-polo
text: It is a fact that all over the country of Cathay there is a kind of black stones existing in beds in the mountains, which they dig out and burn like firewood.
work: Travels, book 2 (the black stones burnt in Cathay: coal)
credit: tr. Henry Yule, 1871 (3rd ed., rev. Henri Cordier, 1903)

speaker: cato-the-elder
text: …much rather be asked, why I have not one, than why I have one.
work: Plutarch, Life of Cato the Elder
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to those who wondered that he had no statue in Rome

speaker: virgil
text: An hour will come, with pleasure to relate Your sorrows past, as benefits of Fate.
work: Aeneid, book 1
note: spoken by Aeneas to his shipwrecked men

speaker: catherine-the-great
text: I had to choose the alternative of perishing with him, or by him, or to save myself, my children, and perhaps the empire also, from the wreck of which all the moral and physical qualities of this Prince made me foresee the danger.
work: Memoirs, on her husband, the Grand Duke Peter (1754)

speaker: gregor-mendel
text: The value and utility of any experiment are determined by the fitness of the material to the purpose for which it is used…
work: Experiments in Plant Hybridisation (1865), introduction
credit: tr. Royal Horticultural Society, revised by William Bateson, 1902

speaker: lorenzo-valla
text: With a brave soul, with utter fidelity, with good hope, the cause of truth must be defended, the cause of justice, the cause of God.
work: On the Forged Donation of Constantine (1440)

speaker: demosthenes
text: It is empire that he desires, and you, as he believes, are his only possible rivals in this.
work: On the Chersonese
note: of Philip II of Macedon

speaker: evliya-celebi
text: I began to think of extensive travels, and to escape from the power of my father, mother, and brethren.
work: Book of Travels (Seyahatname), on his beginnings, 1631

speaker: hippocrates
text: The physician must be able to tell the antecedents, know the present, and foretell the future- must mediate these things, and have two special objects in view with regard to disease, namely, to do good or to do no harm.
work: Epidemics, book 1

speaker: julia-ward-howe
text: In the beauty of the lilies Christ was born across the sea, With a glory in his bosom that transfigures you and me: As He died to make men holy, let us die to make men free, While God is marching on.
work: Battle Hymn of the Republic (The Atlantic Monthly, 1862)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: antonio-pigafetta
text: …they deprived of life our mirror, light, comfort, and true guide. Whilst the Indians were thus overpowering him, several times he turned round towards us to see if we were all in safety…
work: Account of Magellan's voyage: Magellan's death on Mactan, 1521

speaker: epicurus
text: …it is not possible to live pleasantly unless one also lives prudently, and honourably, and justly; and that one cannot live prudently, and honestly, and justly, without living pleasantly…
work: Letter to Menoeceus (Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 10)

speaker: horatio-nelson
text: If this is the reward for a faithful discharge of my duty, I shall be careful, and never stand forward again. But I have done my duty, and have nothing to accuse myself of.
work: Letter from the West Indies (1785), when others were thanked for his seizures
note: as quoted in Southey's Life of Nelson

speaker: cyrus-the-great
text: This my fatherland, which was once of no account in Asia, I leave at the height of power, and of all that I won I think I have lost nothing.
work: Xenophon, Cyropaedia, book 8 (on his deathbed)
note: Xenophon's account, in his idealised life of Cyrus

speaker: elizabeth-cady-stanton
text: The history of mankind is a history of repeated injuries and usurpations on the part of man toward woman, having in direct object the establishment of an absolute tyranny over her.
work: Declaration of Sentiments, Seneca Falls convention (1848)
note: drafted chiefly by her and adopted by the convention

speaker: isidore-of-seville
text: Histories of the heathen do no harm to their readers where they tell what is useful. For many wise men have put past deeds into their histories for the instruction of the present.
work: Etymologies, book 1, chapter 43 (On the usefulness of history)

speaker: maximilien-robespierre
text: The government in a revolution is the despotism of liberty against tyranny.
work: Report on the Principles of Political Morality, February 1794

speaker: baruch-spinoza
text: An emotion, which is a passion, ceases to be a passion, as soon as we form a clear and distinct idea thereof.
work: Ethics, part 5, proposition 3

speaker: hannibal
text: To Pyrrhus; for he first taught the method of encamping; and besides, no one ever showed more exquisite judgment, in choosing his ground, and disposing his posts…
work: Livy, History of Rome, book 35
note: naming the second greatest general, in the same conversation with Scipio Africanus at Ephesus, as Livy reports it

speaker: wang-anshi
text: The incense-stick is burnt to ash, the water-clock is stilled. The midnight breeze blows sharply by, and all around is chilled.
work: A sleepless night in spring (in Giles, A History of Chinese Literature)

speaker: gustave-flaubert
text: Every smile hid a yawn of boredom, every joy a curse, all pleasure satiety, and the sweetest kisses left upon your lips only the unattainable desire for a greater delight.
work: Madame Bovary (1857), part 3

speaker: johannes-kepler
text: …she seemed favourably inclined to the proposal; it is certain that she took time to consider it, but at last she very quietly excused herself.
work: Letter on his search for a second wife, 1613 (Brewster, The Martyrs of Science)
note: of a widow, the first of eleven women he considered; as David Brewster quotes him

speaker: montesquieu
text: Oh! ah! A Persian, is he? Most amazing! However can anybody be a Persian?
work: Persian Letters, letter 30
note: the Parisians' wonder at the visitor Rica, who tells it in the letter
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: aristotle
text: …for as by the completion of it man is the most excellent of all living beings, so without law and justice he would be the worst of all, for nothing is so difficult to subdue as injustice in arms…
work: Politics, book 1

speaker: zhu-xi
text: When God is about to send down calamities upon us, He first raises up the hero whose genius shall finally prevail against those calamities.
work: A saying quoted in Giles, A History of Chinese Literature
note: as a later writer quotes him

speaker: sigmund-freud
text: …the third and most irritating insult is flung at the human mania of greatness by present-day psychological research, which wants to prove to the "I" that it is not even master in its own home…
work: A General Introduction to Psychoanalysis (1917), lecture 18

speaker: isaac-newton
text: …it seems probable to me, that God in the Beginning form'd Matter in solid, massy, hard, impenetrable, moveable Particles…
work: Opticks, query 31

speaker: david-hume
text: Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions, and can never pretend to any other office than to serve and obey them.
work: A Treatise of Human Nature, book 2, part 3, section 3

speaker: homer
text: I would rather be a paid servant in a poor man’s house and be above ground than king of kings among the dead.
work: Odyssey, book 11
note: spoken by the shade of Achilles in the underworld

speaker: yue-fei
text: Such is the jaded condition of those who get little and are easily satisfied, who are over-eager and are easily exhausted.
work: Good Horses, his answer to the emperor (in Giles, Gems of Chinese Literature)

speaker: theodor-herzl
text: The world will be freed by our liberty, enriched by our wealth, magnified by our greatness.
work: The Jewish State (1896), conclusion
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: mary-wollstonecraft
text: Strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and there will be an end to blind obedience…
work: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), chapter 2

speaker: hesiod
text: …potter is angry with potter, and craftsman with craftsman, and beggar is jealous of beggar, and minstrel of minstrel.
work: Works and Days

speaker: samuel-johnson
text: Human life is everywhere a state in which much is to be endured and little to be enjoyed.
work: Rasselas (1759), chapter 11
note: spoken by the poet Imlac

speaker: ibn-tufayl
text: …that he was of a distinct Species from the rest of Animals, and that he was created for another end, and design'd for something greater than what they were capable of.
work: Hayy ibn Yaqzan, section 71
note: of what his hero Hayy concluded about himself

speaker: jose-rizal
text: Why independence, if the slaves of today will be the tyrants of tomorrow? And that they will be such is not to be doubted, for he who submits to tyranny loves it.
work: The Reign of Greed (El Filibusterismo, 1891), ch. 39
note: spoken by Padre Florentino

speaker: sophocles
text: Not to be born at all Is best, far best that can befall, Next best, when born, with least delay To trace the backward way.
work: Oedipus at Colonus
note: sung by the chorus

speaker: william-blake
text: If the doors of perception were cleansed everything would appear to man as it is, infinite.
work: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (c. 1790)

speaker: aeschylus
text: …the inward vice of tyranny, To deem of friends as being secret foes.
work: Prometheus Bound
note: spoken by Prometheus

speaker: jami
text: Philosophers devoid of reason find This world a mere idea of the mind; 'Tis an idea—but they fail to see The great Idealist who looms behind.
work: Lawa'ih (Flashes of Light)
credit: tr. E. H. Whinfield, 1906 (in F. Hadland Davis, The Persian Mystics: Jami, 1908)

speaker: george-eliot
text: What do we live for, if it is not to make life less difficult to each other?
work: Middlemarch (1872), ch. 72
note: spoken by Dorothea Brooke

speaker: william-wordsworth
text: Not in entire forgetfulness, And not in utter nakedness, But trailing clouds of glory do we come From God, who is our home; Heaven lies about us in our infancy!
work: Ode: Intimations of Immortality (1807)

speaker: johann-wolfgang-von-goethe
text: My worthy friend, gray are all theories, And green alone Life’s golden tree.
work: Faust, part 1 (1808), the Study
note: spoken by Mephistopheles to a student

speaker: euripides
text: How are ye blind, Ye treaders down of cities, ye that cast Temples to desolation, and lay waste Tombs, the untrodden sanctuaries where lie The ancient dead; yourselves so soon to die!
work: The Trojan Women
note: spoken by the god Poseidon

speaker: geoffrey-of-monmouth
text: And even the renowned king Arthur himself was mortally wounded; and being carried thence to the isle of Avallon to be cured of his wounds…
work: History of the Kings of Britain, book 11 (the battle of Camlann)
credit: tr. Aaron Thompson, rev. J. A. Giles, 1848
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: pierre-joseph-proudhon
text: Thus, in a given society, the authority of man over man is inversely proportional to the stage of intellectual development which that society has reached…
work: What Is Property? (1840), ch. 5

speaker: friedrich-schiller
text: …man only plays when in the full meaning of the word he is a man, and he is only completely a man when he plays.
work: Letters on the Aesthetic Education of Man (1795), letter 15
credit: anonymous translation (Aesthetical Essays, Bohn edition, 19th century)

speaker: ludwig-van-beethoven
text: Ah! it seemed impossible for me to leave the world until I had produced all that I felt called upon to produce; and so I prolonged this wretched existence.
work: The Heiligenstadt Testament, 6 October 1802

speaker: pindar
text: But evenly ever in sunlight night and day an unlaborious life the good receive, neither with violent hand vex they the earth nor the waters of the sea, in that new world…
work: Olympian Odes, 2
note: of the life of the good after death

speaker: shinran
text: Go forward, O Valiant Souls, seeking the Law though all the worlds fall into flame and ruin, for ye shall have passed beyond birth and death!
work: Wasan (hymns), 29
credit: tr. S. Yamabe and L. Adams Beck, 1921

speaker: mahatma-gandhi
text: As soon as India accepts the doctrine of the sword, my life as an Indian is finished.
work: Speech on non-co-operation, Madras, 12 August 1920
note: from Freedom's Battle (1922)

speaker: wolfgang-amadeus-mozart
text: The time as yet we know not, but that does not disturb me; when God wills it I am ready.
work: Letter to his father on his mother's death, Paris, 9 July 1778

speaker: cesare-beccaria
text: The greater the number of those who understand and have in their hands the sacred code of the laws, the fewer will be the crimes committed…
work: On Crimes and Punishments (1764), chapter 5

speaker: solon
text: So I stood with my shield outstretched, and both were safe in its sight, And I would not that either should triumph, when the triumph was not with right.
work: a poem on his reforms, quoted in Aristotle's Athenian Constitution

speaker: prince-shotoku
text: Decisions on important matters should not be made by one person alone. They should be discussed with many.
work: Seventeen-Article Constitution, 604, article 17 (Nihongi, book 22)
note: the constitution the Nihongi attributes to him
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: albert-einstein
text: At this point an enigma presents itself which in all ages has agitated inquiring minds. How can it be that mathematics, being after all a product of human thought which is independent of experience, is so admirably appropriate to the objects of reality?
work: Geometry and Experience, address to the Prussian Academy of Sciences (1921)
credit: tr. G. B. Jeffery and W. Perrett, 1922

speaker: sappho
text: Now Love masters my limbs and shakes me, fatal creature, bitter-sweet.
work: Fragments

speaker: jane-austen
text: One half of the world cannot understand the pleasures of the other.
work: Emma (1815), ch. 9
note: spoken by Emma Woodhouse

speaker: aristophanes
text: I am walking in the air, and speculating about the sun.
work: The Clouds
note: spoken by Socrates, as the comedy shows him, hanging in a basket

speaker: ibn-arabi
text: When my Beloved appears, With what eye do I see Him? With His eye, not with mine, For none sees Him except Himself.
work: A poem (in Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam)

speaker: mikhail-bakunin
text: The liberty of man consists solely in this: that he obeys natural laws because he has himself recognized them as such, and not because they have been externally imposed upon him by any extrinsic will whatever, divine or human, collective or individual.
work: God and the State (written 1871)

speaker: moliere
text: Upon my word, I have been speaking prose these forty years without being aware of it…
work: The Shopkeeper Turned Gentleman (1670), act 2
note: spoken by Monsieur Jourdain

speaker: jean-racine
text: I know my treason, and I lack the boldness Of those abandon'd women who can taste Tranquillity in crime, and show a forehead All unabash'd.
work: Phaedra (1677), act 3, scene 3
note: spoken by Phaedra

speaker: xenophon
text: The thing is to get them to turn their thoughts to what they mean to do, instead of to what they are likely to suffer.
work: Anabasis, book 3
note: his own advice to the officers of the Ten Thousand after their generals were seized, as he gives it

speaker: pope-gregory-i
text: …for they have an angelic face, and it is meet that such should be co-heirs with the Angels in heaven.
work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History, book 2, chapter 1
note: Bede's account of his words on seeing English boys for sale in Rome

speaker: peter-kropotkin
text: The years that I spent in Siberia taught me many lessons which I could hardly have learned elsewhere. I soon realized the absolute impossibility of doing anything really useful for the masses of the people by means of the administrative machinery.
work: Memoirs of a Revolutionist (1899)

speaker: james-cook
text: They live in a Tranquility which is not disturbed by the Inequality of Condition. The earth and Sea of their own accord furnishes them with all things necessary for Life.
work: Journal of the first voyage, August 1770, on the people of New Holland

speaker: samuel-pepys
text: And in the evening Sir W. Pen and I did dig another, and put our wine in it; and I my Parmazan cheese, as well as my wine and some other things.
work: Diary, 4 September 1666, the Great Fire of London

speaker: plutarch
text: For it does not necessarily follow, that, if a piece of work please for its gracefulness, therefore he that wrought it deserves our admiration.
work: Life of Pericles
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859

speaker: einhard
text: His body was large and strong; his stature tall but not ungainly, for the measure of his height was seven times the length of his own feet.
work: Life of Charlemagne, chapter 22

speaker: leo-tolstoy
text: Art is a human activity, consisting in this, that one man consciously, by means of certain external signs, hands on to others feelings he has lived through, and that other people are infected by these feelings, and also experience them.
work: What Is Art? (1897), ch. 5

speaker: daniel-defoe
text: …mine was the middle state, or what might be called the upper station of low life, which he had found, by long experience, was the best state in the world, the most suited to human happiness…
work: Robinson Crusoe (1719)
note: Crusoe recalling his father's advice

speaker: henry-fielding
text: To treat of the effects of love to you, must be as absurd as to discourse on colours to a man born blind…
work: Tom Jones (1749), book 6, chapter 1

speaker: pompey
text: …more worshiped the rising than the setting sun…
work: Plutarch, Life of Pompey
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: Plutarch's account of his words to Sulla, who had refused him a triumph

speaker: gregory-of-tours
text: …it has often been said by men of our day, that few understand the learned words of the rhetorician but many the rude language of the common people.
work: History of the Franks, first preface

speaker: franklin-d-roosevelt
text: People who are hungry and out of a job are the stuff of which dictatorships are made.
work: State of the Union message (1944)

speaker: oliver-goldsmith
text: I was ever of opinion, that the honest man who married and brought up a large family, did more service than he who continued single, and only talked of population.
work: The Vicar of Wakefield (1766), chapter 1
note: narrated by the vicar, Dr Primrose

speaker: qianlong-emperor
text: …our Celestial Empire possesses all things in prolific abundance and lacks no product within its own borders. There was therefore no need to import the manufactures of outside barbarians in exchange for our own produce.
work: Second edict to King George III, 1793
credit: tr. E. Backhouse and J. O. P. Bland, 1914

speaker: sallust
text: Therefore as the result of riches, luxury and greed, united with insolence, took possession of our young manhood.
work: The War with Catiline, 12

speaker: pope-urban-ii
text: Oh, most valiant soldiers and descendants of invincible ancestors, be not degenerate, but recall the valor of your progenitors.
work: Speech at the Council of Clermont, 1095 (Robert the Monk's version)
note: the speech as Robert the Monk, who was there, retold it some years later

speaker: woodrow-wilson
text: We are to beware of all men who would turn the tasks and the necessities of the nation to their own private profit or use them for the building up of private power.
work: Second Inaugural Address (1917)

speaker: george-berkeley
text: …all the choir of heaven and furniture of the earth, in a word all those bodies which compose the mighty frame of the world, have not any subsistence without a mind…
work: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710), section 6

speaker: gottfried-wilhelm-leibniz
text: Now this connexion or adaptation of all created things to each and of each to all, means that each simple substance has relations which express all the others, and, consequently, that it is a perpetual living mirror of the universe.
work: The Monadology (1714), section 56
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: kalidasa
text: The moon behind the western mount is sinking; The eastern sun is heralded by dawn; From heaven's twin lights, their fall and glory linking, Brave lessons of submission may be drawn.
work: Shakuntala, act 4
note: spoken by a pupil of the hermit Kanva at dawn

speaker: louis-ix-of-france
text: …you should dress well and neatly, so that your wives may love you the better, and your followers esteem you the more.
work: Words to Joinville and Robert de Sorbon (Joinville, Memoirs)
note: as Jean de Joinville recorded them

speaker: rabindranath-tagore
text: Nationalism is a great menace. It is the particular thing which for years has been at the bottom of India's troubles.
work: Nationalism (1917), Nationalism in India

speaker: jeremy-bentham
text: Natural rights is simple nonsense: natural and imprescriptible rights, rhetorical nonsense, -nonsense upon stilts.
work: Anarchical Fallacies (written c. 1796), on the French Declaration of Rights, article 2
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: alexander-von-humboldt
text: There are nations more susceptible of cultivation, more highly civilized, more enobled by mental cultivation than others, but none in themselves nobler than others. All are in like degree designed for freedom…
work: Cosmos, vol. 1 (1845)

speaker: gaius-marius
text: These are my portraits, these my patent of nobility, not left me by inheritance as theirs were, but won by my own innumerable efforts and perils.
work: Speech to the Roman people (Sallust, The Jugurthine War, 85)
note: Sallust's version of his speech; the nobles kept the wax portraits of their ancestors

speaker: thomas-more
text: The Utopians wonder how any man should be so much taken with the glaring doubtful lustre of a jewel or a stone, that can look up to a star or to the sun himself…
work: Utopia, book 2

speaker: swami-vivekananda
text: Ye are the Children of God, the sharers of immortal bliss, holy and perfect beings. Ye divinities on earth — sinners! It is a sin to call a man so; it is a standing libel on human nature.
work: Paper on Hinduism, Parliament of Religions, Chicago, 1893
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: red-jacket
