speaker: pittacus
text: …that it was the part of wise men, before difficult circumstances arose, to provide for their not arising; but that it was the part of brave men to make the best of existing circumstances.
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 1
note: Diogenes Laertius's report of his saying

speaker: ibn-tufayl
text: Our Ancestors, of Happy Memory, tell us, that there is an Island in the Indian Ocean, situate under the Equinoctial, where Men come into the world spontaneously without the help of Father and Mother.
work: Hayy ibn Yaqzan, the opening of the tale

speaker: walter-raleigh
text: I thank my God heartily that He hath brought me into the light to die, and not suffered me to die in the dark prison of the Tower…
work: Speech on the scaffold, 29 October 1618
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: bias-of-priene
text: …that they ought to love one another as if at a future time they would come to hate one another; for that most men were wicked.
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 1
note: Diogenes Laertius's report of his saying

speaker: w-b-yeats
text: But I, being poor, have only my dreams; I have spread my dreams under your feet; Tread softly because you tread on my dreams.
work: He wishes for the Cloths of Heaven (The Wind Among the Reeds, 1899)

speaker: philip-ii-of-macedon
text: O my son, look thee out a kingdom equal to and worthy of thyself, for Macedonia is too little for thee.
work: Plutarch, Life of Alexander
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to his son after the boy tamed the horse Bucephalus; Plutarch's account

speaker: johann-wolfgang-von-goethe
text: When thus I hail the Moment flying: “Ah, still delay—thou art so fair!” Then bind me in thy bonds undying, My final ruin then declare!
work: Faust, part 1 (1808), the pact with Mephistopheles
note: spoken by Faust

speaker: phocion
text: Have I inadvertently said something foolish?
work: Plutarch, Life of Phocion
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to his friends, when the Athenian assembly applauded one of his speeches; Plutarch's account

speaker: sei-shonagon
text: Getting hold of a lot of stories none of which one has read before.
work: The Pillow-Book: Things that make one Happy

speaker: winston-churchill
text: Socialism seeks to pull down wealth; Liberalism seeks to raise up poverty. Socialism would destroy private interests; Liberalism would preserve private interests in the only way in which they can be safely and justly preserved, namely, by reconciling them with public right.
work: Speech at Dundee, 1908 (Liberalism and the Social Problem, 1909)

speaker: marcus-junius-brutus
text: Yes, indeed, we must fly, but not with our feet, but with our hands.
work: Plutarch, Life of Brutus
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: after the defeat at Philippi, meaning to die by his own hand; Plutarch's account

speaker: tao-yuanming
text: Would you know how that is possible? A heart that is distant creates a wilderness round it.
work: Drinking wine, a poem

speaker: shinran
text: Sin is made one with virtue in its essence, even as ice is one with water. The more there is ice, so much the more water is there.
work: Wasan (hymns), 156
credit: tr. S. Yamabe and L. Adams Beck, 1921

speaker: cesare-beccaria
text: Capital punishment is injurious by the example of barbarity it presents.
work: On Crimes and Punishments (1764), chapter 28

speaker: bertrand-russell
text: The value of philosophy is, in fact, to be sought largely in its very uncertainty.
work: The Problems of Philosophy (1912), ch. 15

speaker: galba
text: Strike, if it be for the Romans’ good.
work: Plutarch, Life of Galba
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: offering his throat to the soldiers who killed him in 69 CE; Plutarch's account

speaker: mikhail-bakunin
text: The idea of God implies the abdication of human reason and justice; it is the most decisive negation of human liberty, and necessarily ends in the enslavement of mankind, both in theory and practice.
work: God and the State (written 1871)

speaker: marcus-licinius-crassus
text: …no man was to be accounted rich that could not maintain an army at his own cost and charges…
work: Plutarch, Life of Crassus
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: Plutarch's report of his saying

speaker: khosrow-i
text: Not far from the truth, I think, is the ancient saying that God does not give blessings unmixed, but He mingles them with troubles and then bestows them upon men.
work: To the Roman envoys after the capture of Antioch, 540 (Procopius, History of the Wars, book 2)
note: Procopius' account, which calls the words high-sounding

speaker: luis-de-camoes
text: O you, the boldest of the nations, fir'd By daring pride, by lust of fame inspir'd, Who, scornful of the bow'rs of sweet repose, Through these my waves advance your fearless prows…
work: The Lusiads (1572), canto 5
note: spoken by Adamastor, the giant of the Cape of Storms, to Vasco da Gama's fleet

speaker: cleopatra-vii
text: Nothing could part us whilst we lived, but death seems to threaten to divide us. You, a Roman born, have found a grave in Egypt; I, an Egyptian, am to seek that favor, and none but that, in your country.
work: Plutarch, Life of Antony
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: at Antony's tomb, a captive of Octavian; Plutarch's account

speaker: charlemagne
text: …we began to fear lest perchance, as the skill in writing was less, so also the wisdom for understanding the Holy Scriptures might be much less than it rightly ought to be.
work: Letter to Abbot Baugulf of Fulda (On the Cultivation of Letters)
note: on the poor Latin of the letters monasteries sent him

speaker: daniel-defoe
text: Thus, fear of danger is ten thousand times more terrifying than danger itself, when apparent to the eyes; and we find the burden of anxiety greater, by much, than the evil which we are anxious about…
work: Robinson Crusoe (1719)
note: narrated by Robinson Crusoe

speaker: lysander
text: For where the lion’s skin will not reach, you must patch it out with the fox’s.
work: Plutarch, Life of Lysander
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to those who said the descendants of Heracles should not use deceit in war; Plutarch's account

speaker: soren-kierkegaard
text: What is a poet? An unhappy man who conceals profound anguish in his heart, but whose lips are so fashioned that when sighs and groans pass over them they sound like beautiful music.
work: Either/Or (1843), Diapsalmata
note: from the Diapsalmata, written in the voice of the pseudonymous aesthete "A"

speaker: alcibiades
text: I will make them feel that I am alive.
work: Plutarch, Life of Alcibiades
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: on hearing that the Athenians had condemned him to death; Plutarch's account

speaker: nicias
text: Men make the city and not walls or ships without men in them.
work: Speech to the army in retreat from Syracuse (Thucydides, book 7)
note: Thucydides' account

speaker: emperor-yang-of-sui
text: The evening river is level and motionless— The spring colours just open to their full. Suddenly a wave carries the moon…
work: Poem on the river at evening

speaker: john-knox
text: Conscience, Madam, requires knowledge; and I fear that right knowledge ye have none.
work: History of the Reformation in Scotland, book 4 (modernized edition, 1905)
note: his own account of his interview with Mary, Queen of Scots, 1561

speaker: robert-louis-stevenson
text: Little do ye know your own blessedness; for to travel hopefully is a better thing than to arrive, and the true success is to labour.
work: El Dorado (Virginibus Puerisque, 1881)

speaker: brasidas
text: …remember that zeal, honour, and obedience mark the good soldier, and that this day will make you either free men and allies of Lacedaemon, or slaves of Athens…
work: Speech before the battle of Amphipolis (Thucydides, book 5)
note: Thucydides' account

speaker: w-e-b-du-bois
text: Work, culture, liberty,—all these we need, not singly but together, not successively but together, each growing and aiding each, and all striving toward that vaster ideal that swims before the Negro people, the ideal of human brotherhood…
work: The Souls of Black Folk (1903), chapter 1

speaker: pope-urban-ii
text: You, girt about with the badge of knighthood, are arrogant with great pride; you rage against your brothers and cut each other in pieces. This is not the (true) soldiery of Christ which rends asunder the sheepfold of the Redeemer.
work: Speech at the Council of Clermont, 1095 (Balderic of Dol's version)
note: the speech as Balderic of Dol retold it some years later

speaker: gottfried-wilhelm-leibniz
text: Moreover, it must be confessed that perception and that which depends upon it are inexplicable on mechanical grounds, that is to say, by means of figures and motions.
work: Monadology (1714), section 17
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: tomyris
text: …but if thou shalt not do so, I swear to thee by the Sun, who is lord of the Massagetai, that surely I will give thee thy fill of blood, insatiable as thou art.
work: Herodotus, Histories, book 1 (message to Cyrus, who had captured her son)
note: Herodotus' account

speaker: porus
text: Treat me, O Alexander, in a kingly way!
work: Arrian, Anabasis, book 5
note: asked by the victorious Alexander how he wished to be treated, 326 BCE; Arrian's account

speaker: nero
text: What an artist is now about to perish!
work: Suetonius, Life of Nero, 49
credit: tr. Alexander Thomson, 1796, rev. T. Forester
note: as his grave was dug, 68 CE; Suetonius' account

speaker: alp-arslan
text: I was advised by a sage to humble myself before God; to distrust my own strength; and never to despise the most contemptible foe. I have neglected these lessons; and my neglect has been deservedly punished.
work: His dying words, 1072 (in Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 57)
note: as Gibbon gives them from the Persian historians; he had been stabbed by a prisoner

speaker: john-newton
text: I hope it will always be a subject of humiliating reflection to me, that I was, once, an active instrument, in a business at which my heart now shudders.
work: Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade (1788)

speaker: arthur-conan-doyle
text: How often have I said to you that when you have eliminated the impossible whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth?
work: The Sign of the Four (1890), ch. 6
note: spoken by Sherlock Holmes

speaker: titus
text: My friends, I have lost a day.
work: Suetonius, Life of Titus, 8
credit: tr. Alexander Thomson, 1796, rev. T. Forester
note: on a day when he had done no one a kindness; Suetonius' account

speaker: otho
text: Romans combat here against Romans, and, whether we conquer or are defeated, our country suffers and we commit a crime: victory, to whichever it fall, is gained at her expense.
work: Plutarch, Life of Otho
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to his soldiers after the defeat at Bedriacum, 69 CE, before taking his own life; Plutarch's account

speaker: malik-shah-i
text: I implored the Lord of Hosts that he would take from me my life and crown, if my brother be more worthy than myself to reign over the Moslems.
work: At the tomb of the Imam Riza at Tus, on the eve of battle with his brother (in Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 57)
note: as Gibbon gives it from the Persian historians, answering his vizier

speaker: marquis-de-lafayette
text: When I first learnt the subject of the quarrel, my heart espoused warmly the cause of liberty, and I thought of nothing but of adding also the aid of my banner.
work: Memoirs, on the year 1776
credit: tr. 1837, in the edition published by his family (translator not named)

speaker: david-lloyd-george
text: It is the one thing he discovers has not changed—the world has not learned one single syllable.
work: Where Are We Going? (1923)

speaker: lucius-aemilius-paullus-macedonicus
text: …fortune never conferred any great benefits that were unmixed and unattended with probabilities of reverse.
work: Plutarch, Life of Aemilius Paulus
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to the Roman people after his triumph of 167 BCE, in which days he lost two sons; Plutarch's account

speaker: michelangelo
text: From heaven his spirit came, and robed in clay The realms of justice and of mercy trod, Then rose a living man to gaze on God, That he might make the truth as clear as day.
work: Sonnet on Dante

speaker: agesilaus-ii
text: I know certainly how to humble those who pretend to more power than myself.
work: Plutarch, Life of Agesilaus
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to Lysander, who complained that he knew how to humble his friends; Plutarch's account

speaker: carl-linnaeus
text: If the summer be indeed shorter here than in any other part of the world, it must be allowed, at the same time, to be no where more delightful. I was never in my life in better health than at present.
work: Lachesis Lapponica, the journal of his tour in Lapland (1732)

speaker: yung-wing
text: I was determined that the rising generation of China should enjoy the same educational advantages that I had enjoyed; that through western education China might be regenerated, become enlightened and powerful.
work: My Life in China and America (1909), ch. 5
note: the first Chinese graduate of an American college, Yale 1854

speaker: sulla
text: I give you for guard your father, your brother, your friends and kindred, whose unjust and cruel murder I am now going to revenge…
work: Plutarch, Life of Crassus
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to the young Crassus, who asked for a guard to raise troops in the civil war; Plutarch's account

speaker: william-caxton
text: Lo, what should a man in these days now write, eggs or eyren? Certainly it is hard to please every man because of diversity and change of language.
work: Prologue to the Eneydos (1490)
note: in modernised spelling; on a London mercer who asked for eggs in Kent and was not understood

speaker: gaius-cassius-longinus
text: Bear witness for me, Messala, that I am brought into the same necessity as Pompey the Great was before me, of hazarding the liberty of my country upon one battle…
work: Plutarch, Life of Brutus
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: on the eve of Philippi, 42 BCE; Plutarch's account

speaker: adam-ferguson
text: Every step and every movement of the multitude, even in what are termed enlightened ages, are made with equal blindness to the future; and nations stumble upon establishments, which are indeed the result of human action, but not the execution of any human design.
work: An Essay on the History of Civil Society (1767), part 3

speaker: georges-clemenceau
text: It learns nothing by discourses; could discourses teach the world, the Sermon on the Mount would have been realized long ago.
work: Speech in the debate on socialism with Jean Jaurès, Chamber of Deputies, 1906
credit: tr. in The World's Famous Orations, ed. William Jennings Bryan, 1906 (translator not named)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: mark-antony
text: …for I shall soon be with you; but it distresses me that so great a general should be found of a tardier courage than a woman.
work: Plutarch, Life of Antony
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: believing Cleopatra already dead, before he took his own life; Plutarch's account

speaker: teresa-of-avila
text: …mental prayer is nothing else, in my opinion, but being on terms of friendship with God, frequently conversing in secret with Him Who, we know, loves us.
work: The Life of St. Teresa, chapter 8

speaker: agis-iv
text: …for me, who die innocent, by the lawless act of wicked men. My condition is much better than theirs.
work: Plutarch, Life of Agis
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to an officer weeping at his execution, 241 BCE; Plutarch's account

speaker: harun-al-rashid
text: I have read thy letter, O thou son of an unbelieving mother. Thou shalt not hear, thou shalt behold, my reply.
work: Answer to the emperor Nikephoros I, 803 (in Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 52)
note: as Gibbon gives it; the reply was a campaign into Asia Minor

speaker: emilio-castelar
text: …for the laws of history do not permit a dictatorship to fasten itself upon a people whose faces are lighted by the fires of eloquence.
work: Plea for a Republic, Spanish Constituent Cortes, 1869
credit: tr. in The World's Famous Orations, ed. William Jennings Bryan, 1906 (translator not named)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: eumenes-of-cardia
text: While I am able to wield a sword, I shall think no man greater than myself.
work: Plutarch, Life of Eumenes
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: besieged, when Antigonus required him to address him as his superior; Plutarch's account

speaker: anselm-of-canterbury
text: Up now, slight man! flee, for a little while, your occupations; hide yourself, for a time, from your disturbing thoughts.
work: Proslogion, chapter 1

speaker: polybius
text: …the most instructive, or rather the only, method of learning to bear with dignity the vicissitudes of fortune is to recall the catastrophes of others.
work: Histories, book 1

speaker: pierre-corneille
text: In conquering without danger we triumph without glory.
work: Le Cid (1637), act 2
note: spoken by the Count, Chimène's father, to the young Rodrigo

speaker: vincent-van-gogh
text: And withal he ought to have some feeling for the stars and the infinite heavens. Then it is a joy to live!
work: Letter from Arles, 1888 (The Letters of a Post-Impressionist)

speaker: scipio-aemilianus
text: O Polybius, it is a grand thing, but, I know not how, I feel a terror and dread, lest some one should one day give the same order about my own native city.
work: Polybius, Histories, book 38
note: as he gave the order to burn Carthage, 146 BCE; Polybius, who stood beside him, records it

speaker: faxian
text: When I look back on what I have gone through, my heart is involuntarily moved, and the perspiration flows forth. That I encountered danger and trod the most perilous places, without thinking of or sparing myself, was because I had a definite aim…
work: A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms, closing note
note: his words as a monk who met him in 416 wrote them down

speaker: christopher-marlowe
text: Why, this is hell, nor am I out of it: Think'st thou that I, that saw the face of God, And tasted the eternal joys of heaven, Am not tormented with ten thousand hells, In being depriv'd of everlasting bliss?
work: Doctor Faustus, act 1
note: spoken by Mephistophilis to Faustus

speaker: mehmed-ii
text: The spider has wove his web in the Imperial palace; and the owl hath sung her watch-song on the towers of Afrasiab.
work: In the palace of the emperors, Constantinople, 1453 (in Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 68)
note: a Persian couplet he recited, as Gibbon tells it

speaker: franz-liszt
text: His Polonaises, characterized by an energetic rhythm, galvanize and electrify the torpor of indifference. The most noble traditional feelings of ancient Poland are embodied in them.
work: Life of Chopin (1852), on Chopin's polonaises

speaker: attila
text: No spear shall harm those who are sure to live; and those who are sure to die Fate overtakes even in peace.
work: Speech before the battle of the Catalaunian Plains, 451 (Jordanes, Getica, 39)
note: Jordanes' account, written a century later

speaker: ben-jonson
text: I remember the players have often mentioned it as an honour to Shakspeare, that in his writing (whatsoever he penned) he never blotted out a line. My answer hath been, “Would he had blotted a thousand,” which they thought a malevolent speech.
work: Timber, or Discoveries (1641), on Shakespeare

speaker: croesus
text: Neither is it my city that they are plundering nor my wealth which they are carrying away; for I have no longer any property in these things: but it is thy wealth that they are carrying and driving away.
work: Herodotus, Histories, book 1 (to Cyrus, as the Persians sacked Sardis)
note: Herodotus' account

speaker: timur
text: Who are the true martyrs, of those who are slain on my side, or on that of my enemies?
work: To the doctors of the law at Aleppo, 1400 (in Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 65)
note: as Gibbon tells it; Gibbon calls it a captious question

speaker: heinrich-schliemann
text: But the sight of so many objects, every one of which is of inestimable value to archæology, made me foolhardy, and I never thought of any danger.
work: Troy and Its Remains (1875), on finding the treasure at Hisarlik, 1873

speaker: julian-emperor
text: Can any one be judged innocent if it be enough to make a charge?
work: Ammianus Marcellinus, History, book 18
note: to an orator who asked whether anyone would be found guilty if denial were enough; Ammianus' account

speaker: jeremiah
text: Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?
work: Jeremiah 8:22
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: susan-b-anthony
text: Robbed of the fundamental privilege of citizenship, I am degraded from the status of a citizen to that of a subject…
work: To the judge at her sentencing for voting, Canandaigua, 1873
note: from the trial record printed in the History of Woman Suffrage

speaker: bayezid-i
text: Thy armies are innumerable: be they so; but what are the arrows of the flying Tartar against the cimeters and battle-axes of my firm and invincible Janizaries?
work: Letter to Timur, c. 1400 (in Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 65)
note: as Gibbon gives it; two years later Timur defeated and captured him at Ankara

speaker: francois-fenelon
text: The world is not a phantom, it is the aggregate of all its families; and who can civilize and govern these with a nicer discrimination than women?
work: Treatise on the Education of Daughters (1687)

speaker: ulysses-s-grant
text: I felt like anything rather than rejoicing at the downfall of a foe who had fought so long and valiantly, and had suffered so much for a cause, though that cause was, I believe, one of the worst for which a people ever fought…
work: Personal Memoirs (1885), on the surrender at Appomattox

speaker: xerxes-i
text: Far better is it to have a stout heart always, and suffer one's share of evils, than to be ever fearing what may happen, and never incur a mischance.
work: To his uncle Artabanus at Abydos, 480 BCE (Herodotus, Histories, book 7)
note: Herodotus's account
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: al-mustasim
text: Who is this Holagou that dares to rise against them? If he be desirous of peace, let him instantly depart from the sacred territory; and perhaps he may obtain from our clemency the pardon of his fault.
work: Answer to the envoys of Hulagu, 1257 (in Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 64)
note: as Gibbon gives it; "them" are the Abbasid caliphs, whose throne he said rested on the divine decree; Hulagu took Baghdad and put him to death in 1258

speaker: jakob-bohme
text: Son, when thou canst throw thyself into THAT, where no Creature dwelleth, though it be but for a moment, then thou hearest what God speaketh?
work: Of the Supersensual Life (1622), first dialogue
credit: tr. in the William Law edition of his works (1764-1781), ed. Bernard Holland, 1901
note: spoken by the Master to his disciple

speaker: john-redmond
text: The monarch of this mighty Empire is being crowned, and there are assembled in London representatives from all parts of the Empire to acclaim Edward VII. as the constitutional monarch of these realms. There is only one absentee—Ireland.
work: Speech on the coronation of Edward VII, 1902
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: calgacus
text: To robbery, slaughter, plunder, they give the lying name of empire; they make a solitude and call it peace.
work: Speech before the battle of Mons Graupius (Tacitus, Agricola, 30)
credit: tr. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb, 1877
note: Tacitus' account

speaker: kabir
text: If God be within the mosque, then to whom does this world belong?
work: Songs of Kabir

speaker: harald-fairhair
text: This girl has not spoken or done so much amiss that she should be punished, but rather she should be thanked for her words.
work: Saga of Harald Harfager (Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla)
note: on the girl Gyda, who would not marry him until he ruled all Norway; it moved him to vow he would not cut his hair until he did, as Snorri Sturluson tells it three centuries later

speaker: john-amos-comenius
text: I say, and say it again aloud, that this last is the foundation of all the rest: because we can neither act nor speak wisely, unless we first rightly understand all the things which are to be done, and whereof we are to speak.
work: Orbis Pictus (1658), preface

speaker: pandita-ramabai
text: In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, the educated men of this country are opposed to Female Education and the proper position of woman.
work: Evidence to the Education Commission, 1882 (The High-Caste Hindu Woman, 1887)

speaker: seneca-the-younger
text: Why do we complain of Nature? she has dealt kindly with us. Life is long enough, if you know how to use it.
work: On the Shortness of Life, 2

speaker: john-adams
text: I am well aware of the toil and blood and treasure that it will cost us to maintain this Declaration and support and defend these States. Yet, through all the gloom, I can see the rays of ravishing light and glory.
work: Letter to Abigail Adams, 3 July 1776

speaker: gnaeus-julius-agricola
text: For myself I have long been convinced that neither for an army nor for a general is retreat safe. Better, too, is an honourable death than a life of shame, and safety and renown are for us to be found together.
work: Speech before the battle of Mons Graupius (Tacitus, Agricola, 33)
credit: tr. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb, 1877
note: Tacitus' account; Agricola was his father-in-law

speaker: olaf-iii-of-norway
text: Now I know my own capacity, and how little I am suited to be the leader; so I would rather you should go, with my help and assistance.
work: Words to King Canute the Holy of Denmark (Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Saga of Olaf Kyrre)
note: Snorri Sturluson's account; declining to lead an invasion of England, where his father had fallen

speaker: vladimir-lenin
text: He is no revolutionist who would have the revolution of the proletariat only under the "condition" that it proceed smoothly and in an orderly manner…
work: A Letter to American Workingmen (1918)

speaker: caratacus
text: I had men and horses, arms and wealth. What wonder if I parted with them reluctantly? If you Romans choose to lord it over the world, does it follow that the world is to accept slavery?
work: Speech before Claudius in Rome, 51 CE (Tacitus, Annals, book 12)
credit: tr. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb, 1876
note: Tacitus' account

speaker: arminius
text: Not by treachery, not against pregnant women, but openly against armed men do I wage war. There are still to be seen in the groves of Germany the Roman standards which I hung up to our country's gods.
work: Tacitus, Annals, book 1
credit: tr. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb, 1876
note: after the Romans captured his wife; Tacitus' account

speaker: cnut-the-great
text: I have vowed to God himself, henceforward to reform my life in all things, and justly, and piously to govern the kingdoms and the people subject to me, and to maintain equal justice in all things…
work: Letter to the English from Rome, 1027 (William of Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England, book 2)
credit: tr. John Sharpe, 1815, revised by J. A. Giles, 1847
note: the letter as William of Malmesbury copied it a century later

speaker: samuel-richardson
text: But, O sir! my soul is of equal importance with the soul of a princess; though my quality is inferior to that of the meanest slave.
work: Pamela, or Virtue Rewarded (1740)
note: spoken by Pamela to her master, Mr. B.

speaker: robert-schumann
text: Play strictly in time! The playing of many a virtuoso resembles the walk of an intoxicated person.
work: Advice to Young Musicians (1850)

speaker: sophonisba
text: I accept this nuptial present; nor is it an unwelcome one, if my husband can render me no better service.
work: Livy, History of Rome, book 30
note: on receiving the poison her husband Masinissa sent her so that she would not be led in a Roman triumph, 203 BCE; Livy's account

speaker: theocritus
text: Sweet, meseems, is the whispering sound of yonder pine tree, goatherd, that murmureth by the wells of water; and sweet are thy pipings.
work: Idylls, 1
note: spoken by the shepherd Thyrsis in the poem

speaker: saxo-grammaticus
text: Indeed, they account it a delight to learn and to consign to remembrance the history of all nations, deeming it as great a glory to set forth the excellences of others as to display their own.
work: Gesta Danorum (The Danish History), preface
note: on the Icelanders, whose records he followed

speaker: samuel-de-champlain
text: Of all the most useful and excellent arts, that of navigation has always seemed to me to occupy the first place.
work: Address to the Queen Regent, Voyages (1613)

speaker: booker-t-washington
text: I have learned that success is to be measured not so much by the position that one has reached in life as by the obstacles which he has overcome while trying to succeed.
work: Up from Slavery (1901), chapter 2

speaker: plautus
text: …the parents are the builders-up of the children, and lay the foundation for the children; they raise them up, they carefully train them to strength, and that they may be good both for service and for view before the public.
work: The Haunted House (Mostellaria)
note: spoken by the young Philolaches, comparing a man to a house

speaker: karl-marx
text: The social revolution of the nineteenth century can not draw its poetry from the past, it can draw that only from the future.
work: The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte (1852), ch. 1

speaker: plotinus
text: Withdraw within yourself, and examine yourself. If you do not yet therein discover beauty, do as the artist, who cuts off, polishes, purifies until he has adorned his statue with all the marks of beauty.
work: Enneads, 1.6 (Of Beauty), 9

speaker: leif-erikson
text: We have not failed to land, like Bjarni; now I will give this country a name, and call it Helluland (the land of flat stone).
work: Tale of the Greenlanders (Grænlendinga saga)
note: the saga's account, written down about two centuries later; on the first shore he reached west of Greenland

speaker: roger-williams
text: Boast not proud English, of thy birth and blood Thy Brother Indian is by birth as Good. Of one blood God made Him, and Thee, and All. As wise, as faire, as strong, as personall.
work: A Key into the Language of America (1643), chapter 1

speaker: themistocles
text: We have indeed left our houses and our walls, base fellow, not thinking it fit to become slaves for the sake of things that have no life nor soul…
work: Plutarch, Life of Themistocles
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to a man who mocked the Athenians for abandoning their city to the Persians, 480 BCE; Plutarch's account

speaker: murasaki-shikibu
text: I wish I could be more adaptable and live more gaily in the present world—had I not an extraordinary sorrow—but whenever I hear delightful or interesting things my yearning for a religious life grows stronger.
work: Diary, 1008-1010 (in Diaries of Court Ladies of Old Japan)
credit: tr. Annie Shepley Omori and Kochi Doi, 1920

speaker: fyodor-dostoevsky
text: I tell Thee that man is tormented by no greater anxiety than to find some one quickly to whom he can hand over that gift of freedom with which the ill-fated creature is born.
work: The Brothers Karamazov (1880), book 5, The Grand Inquisitor
note: spoken by the Grand Inquisitor in Ivan Karamazov's poem

speaker: leonidas-i
text: If you understood wherein consisted the happiness of life, you would not covet other men’s; but know that I would rather die for the liberty of Greece than be a monarch over my countrymen.
work: Plutarch, Sayings of the Spartans (Moralia)
credit: tr. several hands, rev. William W. Goodwin, 1870
note: his answer to Xerxes, who offered him the lordship of Greece; Plutarch's collection of sayings

speaker: william-bradford-governor
text: …a great hope & inward zeall they had of laying some good foundation, or at least to make some way therunto, for ye propagating & advancing ye gospell of ye kingdom of Christ in those remote parts of ye world…
work: Of Plymouth Plantation, book 1, chapter 4

speaker: archidamus-iii
text: Let us not mind that, but whether we shall fight bravely and beat our enemies.
work: Plutarch, Sayings of the Spartans (Moralia)
credit: tr. several hands, rev. William W. Goodwin, 1870
note: to those who advised him to fight far from his own country; Plutarch's collection of sayings

speaker: isaac-watts
text: When I survey the wondrous cross On which the Prince of Glory dy'd, My richest gain I count but loss, And pour contempt on all my pride.
work: When I Survey the Wondrous Cross, Hymns and Spiritual Songs (1707)

speaker: aristippus-of-cyrene
text: If all the laws should be abrogated, we should still live in the same manner as we do now.
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 2
note: asked what advantage philosophers had over other men

speaker: erik-the-red
text: I am not fated to discover more countries than this in which we are now settled, and we ought not to bear one another company any longer.
work: Tale of the Greenlanders (Grænlendinga saga)
note: the saga's account, written down about two centuries later; his horse had stumbled as he rode to join his son's voyage

speaker: mark-twain
text: Let us endeavor so to live that when we come to die even the undertaker will be sorry.
work: Pudd'nhead Wilson (1894), chapter 6
note: a motto from "Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar", the novel's chapter headings

speaker: constantius-ii
text: I entreat you to listen attentively to what I will state with all the brevity possible. For the language of truth is always concise and simple.
work: Speech to his army (Ammianus Marcellinus, History, book 14)
note: Ammianus' account

speaker: hugo-grotius
text: There are some things of such a nature, as to contribute, no way, to the support and prolongation of war: things which reason itself requires to be spared even during the heat and continuance of war.
work: On the Law of War and Peace (1625), book 3, chapter 12

speaker: arrian
text: In relating the history of Alexander’s achievements, there are some things which I have been compelled to censure; but I am not ashamed to admire Alexander himself.
work: Anabasis of Alexander, book 7

speaker: caedmon
text: Now must we praise the Maker of the heavenly kingdom, the power of the Creator and His counsel, the deeds of the Father of glory.
work: Hymn, about 670 (Bede, Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 24)
note: the opening of the oldest English poem whose maker is known, which Bede gives in Latin prose and says came to him in a dream

speaker: william-tecumseh-sherman
text: You cannot qualify war in harsher terms than I will. War is cruelty, and you cannot refine it; and those who brought war into our country deserve all the curses and maledictions a people can pour out.
work: Letter to the mayor and councilmen of Atlanta, 12 September 1864 (Memoirs, 1875)

speaker: josephus
text: Yet shall I suit my language to the passions I am under, as to the affairs I describe, and must be allowed to indulge some lamentations upon the miseries undergone by my own country.
work: The Wars of the Jews, preface

speaker: joseph-conrad
text: Did he live his life again in every detail of desire, temptation, and surrender during that supreme moment of complete knowledge?
work: Heart of Darkness (1899)
note: Marlow on Kurtz's last moments

speaker: john-marshall
text: That the power to tax involves the power to destroy; that the power to destroy may defeat and render useless the power to create…
work: Opinion of the Court, McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: jesus
text: Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you…
work: Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 5:44
note: as Matthew's Gospel records his teaching
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: saint-cuthbert
text: …remember at this time to ask me and speak to me concerning all whereof you have need to ask and speak; for, when we part, we shall never again see one another with bodily eyesight in this world.
work: Words to the hermit Herebert at Carlisle (Bede, Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 29)
note: Bede's account of their last meeting

speaker: sun-yat-sen
text: What is true in military warfare is more so in trade warfare.
work: The International Development of China (1922)

speaker: thomas-cranmer
text: To do good unto all men, as much as in you lieth, and to hurt no man, no more than you would hurt your own natural loving brother or sister.
work: His last exhortation before his burning, Oxford, 21 March 1556
note: as Foxe recorded it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: tacitus
text: All this in their ignorance they called civilisation, when it was but a part of their servitude.
work: Agricola, 21
credit: tr. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb, 1877
note: of the Britons taking up Roman dress, baths and banquets

speaker: henrik-ibsen
text: …the spirit of truth and the spirit of freedom--they are the pillars of society.
work: Pillars of Society (1877), closing words
note: spoken by Lona Hessel

speaker: francisco-de-quevedo
text: The death of laughter was the last of all, and surrounded with a throng of people, hasty to believe, and slow to repent, living without fear of justice, and dying without hope of mercy.
work: The Visions (1627), the Vision of Death

speaker: david
text: What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?
work: Psalm 8:4
note: from a psalm the Bible heads "A Psalm of David"
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: belisarius
text: You, however, act as though you were playing at dice, and want to risk all on a single cast; but it is not my custom to choose the short course in preference to the advantageous one.
work: Words to the people of Rome, impatient for battle, 537 (Procopius, History of the Wars, book 5, chapter 28)
note: Procopius' account; he was Belisarius' secretary

speaker: isaiah
text: The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them.
work: Isaiah 11:6
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: mary-shelley
text: Remember that I am thy creature; I ought to be thy Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel, whom thou drivest from joy for no misdeed.
work: Frankenstein (1818), ch. 10
note: spoken by the creature to his maker

speaker: william-morris
text: I do not want art for a few, any more than education for a few, or freedom for a few.
work: The Art of the People, lecture of 1879 (Hopes and Fears for Art, 1882)

speaker: lord-byron
text: There was a sound of revelry by night, And Belgium's capital had gathered then Her Beauty and her Chivalry, and bright The lamps shone o'er fair women and brave men…
work: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, canto 3 (1816), the eve of Waterloo

speaker: sei-shonagon
text: It seems as though people with nice feelings must necessarily be silly, and clever people must always be ill-natured, men and women too. But I suppose really there must be lots of nice, clever people, if only one knew them.
work: The Pillow-Book

speaker: daniel-oconnell
text: My friends, I want nothing for the Irish but their country, and I think the Irish are competent to obtain their own country for themselves.
work: Speech at the Mullaghmast meeting, 1843
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: walter-bagehot
text: Above all things our royalty is to be reverenced, and if you begin to poke about it you cannot reverence it. When there is a select committee on the Queen, the charm of royalty will be gone. Its mystery is its life.
work: The English Constitution (1867), ch. 3, The Monarchy

speaker: herod-the-great
text: Go and search diligently for the young child; and when ye have found him, bring me word again, that I may come and worship him also.
work: Matthew 2:8, to the wise men from the east
note: as Matthew's Gospel tells it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: olaf-ii-of-norway

work: Words to his skalds before the battle of Stiklestad, 1030 (Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Saga of Olaf Haraldson)
note: Snorri Sturluson's account, written two centuries later

speaker: bertrand-russell

work: The Problems of Philosophy (1912), ch. 15

work: Summa Theologica, part 1, question 1, article 1
credit: tr. Fathers of the English Dominican Province, 1920
note: on why revelation was needed besides philosophy

speaker: alphonse-de-lamartine
text: The virtue of the Revolution was in the idea which forced these men on to accomplish it, and not in those who actually accomplished it; all its instruments were vitiated, corrupt, or personal; but the idea was pure, incorruptible, divine.
work: History of the Girondists (1847), book 1

speaker: cao-cao
text: Here is wine, let us sing; For man’s life is short, Like the morning dew, Its best days gone by. But though we would rejoice, Sorrows are hard to forget, What will make us forget them? Wine, and only wine.
work: Short Song (in Giles, A History of Chinese Literature)

speaker: lajos-kossuth
text: That spirit is a power for deeds, but is yet no deed in itself. Despotism and oppression never yet were beaten except by heroic resistance. That is a sad necessity,—but it is a necessity nevertheless.
work: Speech at New York, December 1851 (Select Speeches of Kossuth, 1854)
note: spoken in English, in exile after the Hungarian revolution

speaker: ernest-renan
text: I no longer believe Christianity to be the supernatural summary of all that man can know; but I still believe that life is the most frivolous of things, unless it is regarded as one great and constant duty.
work: Recollections of My Youth (1883)

speaker: nehemiah
text: The God of heaven, he will prosper us; therefore we his servants will arise and build…
work: Nehemiah 2:20, answering those who mocked the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls
note: his own memoir as the Book of Nehemiah gives it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: lorenzo-valla

work: On the Forged Donation of Constantine (1440)
note: of the forger of the Donation of Constantine

speaker: lope-de-vega

work: The New Art of Writing Plays (1609)

speaker: multatuli
text: I ask Thee if it be thine Imperial will that the Havelaars should be bespattered with the mud of Slymerings and Drystubbles; and that thy more than thirty millions of Subjects far away should be ill-treated and should suffer extortion in THY name?
work: Max Havelaar (1860), closing words
note: addressed to King William III of the Netherlands, in whose name the Dutch East Indies were ruled

speaker: john-knox
text: Madam, as right religion took neither original strength nor authority from worldly princes, but from the Eternal God alone, subjects are not bound to frame their religion according to the appetites of their princes.
work: History of the Reformation in Scotland, book 4 (modernized edition, 1905)
note: his own account of his interview with Mary, Queen of Scots, 1561

speaker: cyrus-the-great
text: I have never yet been afraid of any men, who have a set place in the middle of their city, where they come together to cheat each other and forswear themselves.
work: To a Spartan herald who warned him not to harm the Greek cities of Asia (Herodotus, Histories, book 1)
note: Herodotus's account, who says he meant the market-places of the Greeks, unknown to the Persians
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: wang-anshi
text: Dear me! he was but the leader of cock-crowing, cur-stealing swashbucklers--men of genius in no sense were they.
work: A False Estimate, on Lord Mengchang (in Giles, Gems of Chinese Literature)
note: of a lord praised for the clever retainers who helped him escape from Qin by crowing like a cock

speaker: henry-wadsworth-longfellow
text: Lives of great men all remind us We can make our lives sublime, And, departing, leave behind us Footprints on the sands of time…
work: A Psalm of Life (1838)

speaker: maximilien-robespierre
text: It is with regret that I utter this fatal truth. But Louis must die, because the country must live.
work: Speech to the National Convention against a trial for Louis XVI, 3 December 1792
credit: tr. in The World's Famous Orations, ed. William Jennings Bryan, 1906 (translator not named)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: pedro-calderon-de-la-barca
text: The king dreams he is a king, And in this delusive way Lives and rules with sovereign sway; All the cheers that round him ring, Born of air, on air take wing.
work: Life Is a Dream (1635), act 2
note: spoken by Prince Sigismund

speaker: aristotle
text: …the roots of education were bitter, but the fruit sweet.
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 5
note: a saying attributed to him by Diogenes Laertius

speaker: zhu-xi
text: And I thought how much I should like to bring back with me portraits of the various great and good, but unknown, men I might be fortunate enough to meet with on the way.
work: Testimonial for the portrait painter Kuo Kung-chen (in Giles, Gems of Chinese Literature)

speaker: arthur-conan-doyle
text: It is a capital mistake to theorise before one has data. Insensibly one begins to twist facts to suit theories, instead of theories to suit facts.
work: A Scandal in Bohemia (1891)
note: spoken by Sherlock Holmes

speaker: john-the-baptist
text: O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
work: Matthew 3:7, to the Pharisees and Sadducees who came to his baptism
note: as Matthew's Gospel records it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: jose-rizal
text: In order to read the destiny of a people, it is necessary to open the book of its past…
work: The Philippines a Century Hence (1889)

speaker: mary-mother-of-jesus
text: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word.
work: Luke 1:38, to the angel of the Annunciation
note: as Luke's Gospel records it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: oswald-of-northumbria
text: Let us all kneel, and together beseech the true and living God Almighty in His mercy to defend us from the proud and cruel enemy; for He knows that we have undertaken a just war for the safety of our nation.
work: Words before the battle of Heavenfield, 634 (Bede, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 2)
note: Bede's account; he had raised a wooden cross on the field

speaker: william-pitt-the-elder
text: If I were an American, as I am an Englishman, while a foreign troop was landed in my country, I never would lay down my arms—never—never—never.
work: Speech in the House of Lords, 18 November 1777
note: as the parliamentary reports reconstructed it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: w-b-yeats
text: I will arise and go now, for always night and day I hear lake water lapping with low sounds by the shore; While I stand on the roadway, or on the pavements gray, I hear it in the deep heart's core.
work: The Lake Isle of Innisfree (1890)

speaker: friedrich-schiller
text: One pen-stroke now, One motion of your hand, can new create The earth! but grant us liberty of thought.
work: Don Carlos (1787), act 3
note: spoken by the Marquis of Posa to King Philip II

speaker: winston-churchill
text: I look forward to the universal establishment of minimum standards of life and labour, and their progressive elevation as the increasing energies of production may permit.
work: Liberalism and the Social Problem (1909), speeches

speaker: elijah
text: How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him.
work: 1 Kings 18:21, to the people on Mount Carmel
note: as the First Book of Kings tells it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: abd-al-rahman-iii
text: In this situation, I have diligently numbered the days of pure and genuine happiness which have fallen to my lot: they amount to Fourteen:—O man! place not thy confidence in this present world!
work: Memorial found among his papers after his death, 961 (Gibbon, Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, chapter 52)
note: as Edward Gibbon renders it from the Arabic historians through Cardonne's French

speaker: wolfgang-amadeus-mozart
text: GOD be praised! My opera was given yesterday, the 13th, and proved so successful that I cannot possibly describe all the tumult.
work: Letter to his mother on the first night of La finta giardiniera, Munich, 14 January 1775

speaker: solon
text: …that laws were like cobwebs—for that if any trifling or powerless thing fell into them, they held it fast; but if a thing of any size fell into them, it broke the meshes and escaped.
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 1
note: Diogenes Laertius's report of his saying

speaker: moliere
text: Ah! How well the man speaks! Come near, let me embrace you for this last saying. It is the finest sentence that I have ever heard in my life: "We must live to eat, and not eat to live." No; that isn't it.
work: The Miser (1668), act 3
note: spoken by the miser Harpagon

speaker: ramon-llull
text: Long and perilous are the paths by which the Lover seeks his Beloved. They are peopled by cares, sighs and tears. They are lit up by love.
work: The Book of the Lover and the Beloved, verse 2 (from Blanquerna, about 1283)

speaker: machado-de-assis
text: The other men read but a chapter of life; you have read the whole book. What does one chapter know of the other chapter? Nothing. But he who has read them all, connects them and concludes.
work: Life (1886), a dialogue in Brazilian Tales
note: spoken by Prometheus to Ahasverus, the Wandering Jew

speaker: ahab
text: Let not him that girdeth on his harness boast himself as he that putteth it off.
work: 1 Kings 20:11, his answer to the boasts of the king of Aram
note: as the First Book of Kings tells it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: pope-gregory-i
text: Choose, therefore, from every Church those things that are pious, religious, and right, and when you have, as it were, made them up into one bundle, let the minds of the English be accustomed thereto.
work: Answers to Augustine of Canterbury (Bede, Ecclesiastical History, book 1, chapter 27)
note: on which customs the new English Church should keep, preserved by Bede

speaker: oliver-cromwell
text: Liberty of conscience, and liberty of the subject,—two as glorious things to be contended for as any that God hath given us…
work: Speech at the opening of the first Protectorate Parliament, 4 September 1654
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: soren-kierkegaard
text: Let others complain that the times are wicked. I complain that they are paltry; for they are without passion. The thoughts of men are thin and frail like lace, and they themselves are feeble like girl lace-makers.
work: Either/Or (1843), Diapsalmata
note: from the Diapsalmata, written in the voice of the pseudonymous aesthete "A"

speaker: rehoboam
text: My father made your yoke heavy, and I will add to your yoke: my father also chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.
work: 1 Kings 12:14, answering the northern tribes at Shechem
note: as the First Book of Kings tells it; the answer split the kingdom
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: pompey
text: It behoves us, who are mortals born, to endure these events, and to try fortune yet again; neither is it any less possible to recover our former state, than it was to fall from that into this.
work: Plutarch, Life of Pompey
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to his wife Cornelia after the defeat at Pharsalus; Plutarch's account

speaker: robert-louis-stevenson
text: Extreme busyness, whether at school or college, kirk or market, is a symptom of deficient vitality; and a faculty for idleness implies a catholic appetite and a strong sense of personal identity.
work: An Apology for Idlers (Virginibus Puerisque, 1881)

speaker: cornplanter
text: When the Sun goes down he opens his heart before God, and earlier than the sun appears upon the hills, he gives thanks for his protection during the night…
work: Speech to President Washington, Philadelphia, 1790
note: speaking of himself; as printed in John Niles Hubbard's account of Red Jacket (1886)

speaker: jezebel
text: Dost thou now govern the kingdom of Israel? arise, and eat bread, and let thine heart be merry: I will give thee the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.
work: 1 Kings 21:7, to her husband, when Naboth would not sell his vineyard
note: as the First Book of Kings tells it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: marie-de-france
text: When the minstrel tells his tale, let the folk about the fire heed him willingly. For his part the singer must be wary not to spoil good music with unseemly words.
work: The Lay of Gugemar, prologue

speaker: jehu
text: What hast thou to do with peace? turn thee behind me.
work: 2 Kings 9:18, to the king's horseman who rode out to meet him
note: as the Second Book of Kings tells it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: benjamin-disraeli
text: The genealogy of Experience is brief; for Experience is the child of Thought, and Thought is the child of Action. We cannot learn men from books…
work: Vivian Grey (1826), book 5

speaker: sojourner-truth
text: …if the Lord comes and burns-as you say he will-I am not going away; I am going to stay here and stand the fire, like Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego!
work: The Narrative of Sojourner Truth (1850), to the Millerites at a camp meeting
note: as told to Olive Gilbert, who wrote the Narrative

speaker: sappho
text: Evening, thou that bringest all that bright morning scattered; thou bringest the sheep, the goat, the child back to her mother.
work: Fragments

speaker: henry-iv-holy-roman-emperor
text: …through wealth you have obtained favor; through favor, the power of the sword; and through the power of the sword, the papal seat, which is the seat of peace; and then from the seat of peace you have expelled peace.
work: Letter to Pope Gregory VII, January 1076
credit: tr. Oliver J. Thatcher and Edgar H. McNeal, 1905
note: written for the synod of Worms that declared the pope deposed

speaker: peter-kropotkin
text: With many large divisions of the animal kingdom mutual aid is the rule.
work: Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution (1902), ch. 1

speaker: booker-t-washington
text: I would permit no man, no matter what his colour might be, to narrow and degrade my soul by making me hate him.
work: Up from Slavery (1901), chapter 10, on a lesson from General Armstrong

speaker: red-jacket
text: …now you have grown to be a mighty tree, whose top reaches the clouds, and whose branches overspread the whole land; whilst we, who were then the tall pine of the forest, have become the feeble plant and need your protection.
work: At a treaty council, 1822 or 1823
note: as given by William L. Stone and quoted in J. N. Hubbard's account of Red Jacket (1886)

speaker: snorri-sturluson
text: The stars shall be Hurled from heaven. Then it shall come to pass that the earth and the mountains will shake so violently that trees will be torn up by the roots, the mountains will topple down…
work: Prose Edda, Gylfaginning, the Ragnarok
note: the end of the world in Norse myth, as told to King Gylfi in the dialogue

speaker: hezekiah
text: Is it not good, if peace and truth be in my days?
work: 2 Kings 20:19, on hearing the prophecy that Babylon would plunder his house
note: as the Second Book of Kings tells it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: david-hume
text: Be a philosopher; but, amidst all your philosophy, be still a man.
work: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, section 1
note: the counsel he gives in the voice of Nature

speaker: marquis-de-lafayette
text: At eight years of age, my heart beat when I heard of a hyena that had done some injury, and caused still more alarm, in our neighbourhood, and the hope of meeting it was the object of all my walks.
work: Memoirs, on his childhood
credit: tr. 1837, in the edition published by his family (translator not named)

speaker: david-lloyd-george
text: Was the devil numbered amongst the slain in the last war? I have never seen his name in any casualty list.
work: Where Are We Going? (1923)

speaker: harald-hardrada
text: The Englishmen shall have a hard fray of it before we give ourselves up for lost.
work: Words at Stamford Bridge, 1066 (Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Saga of Harald Hardrade)
note: Snorri Sturluson's account, written a century and a half later

speaker: agesilaus-ii
text: How much rather had I have so brave a man my friend than mine enemy.
work: Plutarch, Life of Agesilaus
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to the Persian satrap Pharnabazus; Plutarch's account

speaker: samuel-johnson
text: Depend upon it, Sir, when a man knows he is to be hanged in a fortnight, it concentrates his mind wonderfully.
work: In conversation, 19 September 1777 (Boswell, Life of Johnson)
note: Boswell's account

speaker: seneca-the-younger
text: Unbroken prosperity cannot bear a single blow; but he who has waged an unceasing strife with his misfortunes has gained a thicker skin by his sufferings, yields to no disaster, and even though he fall yet fights on his knee.
work: On Providence, 2

speaker: william-bradford-governor
text: If they looked behind them, ther was ye mighty ocean which they had passed, and was now as a maine barr & goulfe to seperate them from all ye civill parts of ye world.
work: Of Plymouth Plantation, book 1, chapter 9

speaker: prince-shotoku
text: Be not envious. For if we envy others, they in turn will envy us. The evils of envy know no limit.
work: Seventeen-Article Constitution, 604, article 14 (Nihongi, book 22)
note: the constitution the Nihongi attributes to him
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: muhammad-iqbal
text: The moral and religious ideal of man is not self-negation but self-affirmation, and he attains to this ideal by becoming more and more individual, more and more unique.
work: Statement of his philosophy, in R. A. Nicholson's introduction to The Secrets of the Self (1920)

speaker: maimonides
text: …when man is able to comprehend certain things, it does not follow that he must be able to comprehend everything.
work: The Guide for the Perplexed, part 1

speaker: adam-ferguson
text: Manufactures, accordingly, prosper most where the mind is least consulted, and where the workshop may, without any great effort of imagination, be considered as an engine, the parts of which are men.
work: An Essay on the History of Civil Society (1767), part 4

speaker: mark-twain
text: It was wonderful to find America, but it would have been more wonderful to miss it.
work: Pudd'nhead Wilson (1894), conclusion
note: a motto from "Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar", the novel's chapter headings

speaker: xenophanes
text: Yes, and if oxen and horses or lions had hands, and could paint with their hands, and produce works of art as men do, horses would paint the forms of the gods like horses, and oxen like oxen…
work: Fragments (Burnet 15)

speaker: einhard
text: He had a great love for foreigners, and took such pains to entertain them that their numbers were justly reckoned to be a burden not only to the palace but to the kingdom at large.
work: Life of Charlemagne, chapter 21

speaker: ludwig-van-beethoven
text: I shall strive if possible to set Fate at defiance, although there must be moments in my life when I cannot fail to be the most unhappy of God's creatures.
work: Letter to Franz Wegeler, 1801, on his deafness

speaker: hans-christian-andersen
text: The history of my life will say to the world what it says to me—There is a loving God, who directs all things for the best.
work: The True Story of My Life (1847)

speaker: josephus
text: It is a brave thing to die in war; but so that it be according to the law of war, by the hand of conquerors.
work: To his companions in the cave at Jotapata, 67 (The Jewish War, book 3)
note: his own account; they had resolved to kill themselves rather than surrender

speaker: louis-ix-of-france
text: I would gladly be branded with a hot iron, on condition that all lewd oaths were done away with out of my kingdom.
work: Words recorded by Joinville (Joinville, Memoirs)
note: as his friend Jean de Joinville recorded them

speaker: robert-boyle
text: I now mean by Elements, as those Chymists that speak plainest do by their Principles, certain Primitive and Simple, or perfectly unmingled bodies…
work: The Sceptical Chymist (1661), part 6
note: spoken by Carneades, the sceptic of the dialogue

speaker: empedocles
text: Hear first the four roots of all things: shining Zeus, life-bringing Hera, Aidoneus, and Nestis whose tear-drops are a well-spring to mortals.
work: Fragments (Burnet 6)

speaker: saxo-grammaticus
text: Men who though they lacked acquaintance with, the speech of Rome, were yet seized with such a passion for bequeathing some record of their history, that they encompassed huge boulders instead of scrolls, borrowing rocks for the usage of books.
work: Gesta Danorum (The Danish History), preface
note: on the runestones of the early Danes

speaker: vincent-van-gogh
text: But when shall I paint the starry heavens?—that picture which is always in my mind?
work: Letter from Arles, 1888 (The Letters of a Post-Impressionist)

speaker: jesus
text: …why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?
work: Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 7:3
note: as Matthew's Gospel records his teaching
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: christiaan-huygens
text: It is always possible to attain thereby to a degree of probability which very often is scarcely less than complete proof.
work: Treatise on Light (1690), preface

speaker: louis-pasteur
text: …two contrary laws seem to be wrestling with each other nowadays; the one, a law of blood and of death, ever imagining new means of destruction and forcing nations to be constantly ready for the battlefield—the other, a law of peace, work and health…
work: Speech at the opening of the Pasteur Institute, 1888 (René Vallery-Radot, The Life of Pasteur)

speaker: giovanni-boccaccio
text: No field was ever so well tilled but therein or nettles or thistles or somewhat of briers or other weeds might be found mingled with the better herbs.
work: The Decameron, the author's conclusion
note: answering readers who found some stories had been better left out

speaker: roger-williams
text: An enforced uniformity of religion throughout a nation or civil state, confounds the civil and religious, denies the principles of Christianity and civility, and that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh.
work: The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution (1644), preface

speaker: anaxagoras
text: All other things partake in a portion of everything, while Nous is infinite and self-ruled, and is mixed with nothing, but is alone, itself by itself.
work: Fragments (Burnet 12)

speaker: frederick-douglass
text: What to the American slave is your Fourth of July? I answer, a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.
work: What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?, speech at Rochester (1852)

speaker: thomas-more
text: They have no lawyers among them, for they consider them as a sort of people whose profession it is to disguise matters and to wrest the laws…
work: Utopia, book 2, on the laws of the Utopians
note: spoken by the traveller Raphael Hythloday in the dialogue

speaker: murasaki-shikibu
text: On moonlight nights in autumn, when I am hopelessly sad, I often go out on the balcony and gaze dreamily at the moon.
work: Diary, 1008-1010 (in Diaries of Court Ladies of Old Japan)
credit: tr. Annie Shepley Omori and Kochi Doi, 1920

speaker: thales-of-miletus
text: God is the most ancient of all things, for he had no birth: the world is the most beautiful of things, for it is the work of God: place is the greatest of things, for it contains all things…
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 1
note: sayings attributed to him by Diogenes Laertius

speaker: walter-raleigh
text: But in this I speak now, what have I to do with kings? I have nothing to do with them, neither do I fear them. I have now to do with God…
work: Speech on the scaffold, 29 October 1618
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: harriet-tubman
text: I was de conductor ob de Underground Railroad for eight years, an' I can say what mos' conductors can't say—I nebber run my train off de track an' I nebber los' a passenger.
work: To a women's suffrage meeting in Rochester (Harriet, the Moses of Her People, 1886)
note: as Sarah Bradford recorded it

speaker: alvar-nunez-cabeza-de-vaca
text: Those people love their offspring the most of any in the world, and treat them with the greatest mildness.
work: The Narrative of Alvar Nuñez Cabeza de Vaca (1542), on the peoples of the Texas coast

speaker: pittacus
text: Even the Gods cannot strive against necessity.
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 1
note: a saying attributed to him by Diogenes Laertius

speaker: william-lloyd-garrison
text: My country is the world! my countrymen are all mankind…
work: Motto of The Liberator

speaker: frederick-the-great
text: Gentlemen, I am undertaking a war in which I have no allies but your valor and your good will. My cause is just; my resources are what we ourselves can do; and the issue lies in fortune.
work: Address to his generals before invading Silesia, December 1740
credit: tr. in The World's Famous Orations, ed. William Jennings Bryan, 1906 (translator not named)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: khosrow-i
text: But when I behold the massacre of such a multitude of men, and the victory thus drenched with blood, there arises in me no sense of the delight that should follow my achievement.
work: To the Roman envoys after the capture of Antioch, 540 (Procopius, History of the Wars, book 2)
note: Procopius' account, which calls the words high-sounding

speaker: tao-yuanming
text: White hair covers my temples, I am wrinkled and seared beyond repair, And though I have got five sons, They all hate paper and brush.
work: Blaming Sons

speaker: brasidas
text: There is nothing so little but it may preserve itself, if it dares resist the invaders.
work: Plutarch, Sayings of the Spartans (Moralia)
credit: tr. several hands, rev. William W. Goodwin, 1870
note: after a mouse he caught among some figs bit him and got away; Plutarch's collection of sayings

speaker: w-e-b-du-bois
text: To be a poor man is hard, but to be a poor race in a land of dollars is the very bottom of hardships.
work: The Souls of Black Folk (1903), chapter 1

speaker: pope-gregory-vii
text: He who attempts to destroy the honor of the church should be deprived of such honor as he may have held.
work: Sentence deposing and excommunicating Henry IV, Lenten synod, 1076
credit: tr. Oliver J. Thatcher and Edgar H. McNeal, 1905

speaker: ethan-allen
text: In the name of the great Jehovah, and the Continental Congress.
work: Narrative of his captivity (1779), the capture of Fort Ticonderoga, 10 May 1775
note: his answer when the British commander asked by what authority he demanded the fort

speaker: sol-plaatje
text: Is it to be thought that God is using the South African Parliament to hound us out of our ancestral homes in order to quicken our pace heavenward? But go from where to heaven?
work: Native Life in South Africa (1916), on the Natives' Land Act

speaker: john-newton
text: I am bound, in conscience, to take shame to myself by a public confession, which, however sincere, comes too late to prevent, or repair, the misery and mischief to which I have, formerly, been accessary.
work: Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade (1788)

speaker: josiah
text: …great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book…
work: 2 Kings 22:13, when the book of the law was found in the Temple
note: as the Second Book of Kings tells it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: pope-innocent-iii
text: Now just as the moon derives its light from the sun and is indeed lower than it in quantity and quality, in position and in power, so too the royal power derives the splendor of its dignity from the pontifical authority....
work: Letter to the prefect Acerbius and the nobles of Tuscany, 1198
credit: tr. Oliver J. Thatcher and Edgar H. McNeal, 1905

speaker: emir-abdelkader
text: …all that, as you well know, is nothing but the fulfilment of the principles of our sacred law and of the dictates of humanity. Indeed, our law is the confirmation of all the best qualities, and embraces all virtues as a collar encircles the neck.
work: Letter to Imam Shamil on the defence of the Christians of Damascus, 1860
note: from Churchill's Life of Abdel Kader

speaker: ezra
text: O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee, my God: for our iniquities are increased over our head, and our trespass is grown up unto the heavens.
work: Ezra 9:6, his prayer at the evening sacrifice
note: as the Book of Ezra gives his words
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: leonidas-i
text: Marry brave men, and bear them brave children.
work: Plutarch, Sayings of the Spartans (Moralia)
credit: tr. several hands, rev. William W. Goodwin, 1870
note: to his wife Gorgo, who asked what he left her to do as he marched to Thermopylae; Plutarch's collection of sayings

speaker: al-biruni
text: Think of Socrates when he opposed the crowd of his nation as to their idolatry and did not want to call the stars gods!
work: India (Tahqiq ma li-l-Hind), chapter 2

speaker: carl-linnaeus
text: I witnessed with pleasure the supreme tranquillity enjoyed by the inhabitants of this sequestered country.
work: Lachesis Lapponica, the journal of his tour in Lapland (1732)

speaker: wilfrid-laurier
text: Nature had endowed him with many brilliant qualities, but nature had denied him that supreme quality without which all other qualities, however brilliant, are of no avail. Nature had denied him a well-balanced mind.
work: Speech in the House of Commons on Louis Riel, 1886
note: as quoted in O. D. Skelton, The Day of Sir Wilfrid Laurier (1916)

speaker: cyrus-the-younger
text: See then that you prove yourselves to be men worthy of the liberty which you possess, and which I envy you. Liberty—it is a thing which, be well assured, I would choose in preference to all my other possessions, multiplied many times.
work: To his Greek officers before the battle of Cunaxa, 401 BCE (Xenophon, Anabasis, book 1)
note: Xenophon's account

speaker: isaac-watts
text: How doth the little busy bee Improve each shining hour, And gather honey all the day From every opening flower!
work: Against Idleness and Mischief, Divine Songs for Children (1715)

speaker: georges-clemenceau
text: You have the magic power of evoking fairy palaces with your wand, while I am as some modest laborer on a cathedral who obscurely carries a stone to the august edifice he shall never see.
work: Speech in the debate on socialism with Jean Jaurès, Chamber of Deputies, 1906
credit: tr. in The World's Famous Orations, ed. William Jennings Bryan, 1906 (translator not named)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: darius-iii
text: Alas! how great is the calamity of the Persians! Was it not enough that their king’s consort and sister was a prisoner in her lifetime, but she must, now she is dead also, be but meanly and obscurely buried?
work: On hearing of his wife's death in Alexander's camp (Plutarch, Life of Alexander)
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: Plutarch's account

speaker: mongke
text: …believe that there is only one God, by whom we live and by whom we die, and for whom we have an upright heart.
work: Words to William of Rubruck at Karakorum, Pentecost 1254
note: as the Franciscan envoy William of Rubruck, whom he received at Karakorum in 1254, recorded his words

speaker: shapur-ii
text: Even your own ancient records bear witness that my ancestors possessed all the country up to the Strymon and the frontier of Macedonia.
work: Letter to the emperor Constantius II, 358 (Ammianus Marcellinus, History, book 17)
note: the letter as Ammianus gives it

speaker: ramon-llull
text: If we understand not one another’s speech, we may make ourselves understood by love; for in thy song I see my Beloved before mine eyes.
work: The Book of the Lover and the Beloved, verse 26 (from Blanquerna, about 1283)
note: spoken by the Lover to a bird singing in the garden

speaker: henry-wadsworth-longfellow
text: Thou, too, sail on, O Ship of State! Sail on, O UNION, strong and great! Humanity with all its fears, With all the hopes of future years, Is hanging breathless on thy fate!
work: The Building of the Ship (1849)

speaker: emperor-wu-of-han
text: The sound of her silk skirt has stopped. On the marble pavement dust grows. Her empty room is cold and still. Fallen leaves are piled against the doors. Longing for that lovely lady How can I bring my aching heart to rest?
work: Li Fu-jen, on the death of his consort Lady Li

speaker: pierre-corneille
text: O rage! O despair! O inimical old age! Have I then lived so long only for this disgrace? And have I grown grey in warlike toils, only to see in one day so many of my laurels wither?
work: Le Cid (1637), act 1
note: spoken by Don Diego, Rodrigo's father, after he has been struck

speaker: emilio-castelar
text: Cato committed suicide because he found a Caesar. Radicals of Spain, do not commit suicide because you can not find a monarch.
work: Plea for a Republic, Spanish Constituent Cortes, 1869, closing words
credit: tr. in The World's Famous Orations, ed. William Jennings Bryan, 1906 (translator not named)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: faxian
text: I did not quit the family in compliance with my father’s wishes, but because I wished to be far from the dust and vulgar ways of life. This is why I chose monkhood.
work: His reply as a boy to an uncle who urged him to go home to his mother (Memoirs of Eminent Monks, 519, in Legge's introduction)
note: as the Memoirs of Eminent Monks record it

speaker: john-ii-of-france
text: To whom shall I yield me? Where is my cousin the prince of Wales? If I might see him, I would speak with him.
work: Words at his capture, battle of Poitiers, 1356 (Froissart, Chronicles)
note: Froissart's account

speaker: aphra-behn
text: It may be easily guess’d, in what Manner the Prince resented this Indignity, who may be best resembled to a Lion taken in a Toil; so he raged, so he struggled for Liberty, but all in vain…
work: Oroonoko, or The Royal Slave (1688)
note: the narrator, on the prince seized by an English slave captain

speaker: john-a-macdonald
text: A British subject I was born, a British subject I will die.
work: Address to the electors of Canada, 1891
note: as quoted in Joseph Pope, The Day of Sir John Macdonald (1915)

speaker: julian-emperor
text: For, to any impartial judge, that man is base and cowardly who seeks to die when he ought not, or who avoids death when it is seasonable for him.
work: Ammianus Marcellinus, History, book 25
note: dying of his wound in Persia, 363 CE; Ammianus, who served in the campaign, records it

speaker: timur
text: Yet by my arm has the Almighty been pleased to subdue the kingdoms of Iran, Touran, and the Indies.
work: To the doctors of the law at Aleppo, 1400 (in Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 65)
note: as Gibbon tells it; just before, he had called himself a poor, lame, decrepit mortal

speaker: lili-uokalani
text: That I yield to the superior force of the United States of America, whose Minister Plenipotentiary, His Excellency John L. Stevens, has caused United States troops to be landed at Honolulu, and declared that he would support the said Provisional Government.
work: Protest on the overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy, 17 January 1893
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: francois-fenelon
text: Those who are instructed and busied in serious employments, have, in general, but a moderate curiosity.
work: Treatise on the Education of Daughters (1687)

speaker: jeremiah
text: They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
work: Jeremiah 6:14, against the prophets and priests of Jerusalem
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: sei-shonagon
text: When one sends a poem or a kayeshi (‘return-poem’) to someone and, after it has gone, thinks of some small alteration—perhaps only a couple of letters—that would have improved it.
work: The Pillow-Book: Annoying Things

speaker: susan-b-anthony
text: I shall never pay a dollar of your unjust penalty.
work: To the judge at her sentencing for voting, Canandaigua, 1873
note: from the trial record printed in the History of Woman Suffrage

speaker: thomas-paine
text: Society in every state is a blessing, but government even in its best state is but a necessary evil; in its worst state an intolerable one…
work: Common Sense (1776)

speaker: cambyses-ii
text: Ah! truly, do what they may, it is impossible for men to turn aside the coming fate.
work: To the Persian nobles, dying, 522 BCE (Herodotus, Histories, book 3)
note: Herodotus's account; he had killed his brother on the strength of a dream
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: ulysses-s-grant
text: I feel that we are on the eve of a new era, when there is to be great harmony between the Federal and Confederate.
work: Personal Memoirs (1885), conclusion, written as he was dying

speaker: bertrand-russell
