text: A life lived in this spirit—the spirit that aims at creating rather than possessing—has a certain fundamental happiness, of which it cannot be wholly robbed by adverse circumstances.
work: Proposed Roads to Freedom (1918), ch. 8

speaker: kabir
text: I laugh when I hear that the fish in the water is thirsty…
work: Songs of Kabir

speaker: olaudah-equiano
text: For I will not suppose that the dealers in slaves are born worse than other men—No; it is the fatality of this mistaken avarice, that it corrupts the milk of human kindness and turns it into gall.
work: The Interesting Narrative (1789), chapter 5

speaker: edward-the-black-prince
text: Sir, for God's sake make none evil nor heavy cheer, though God this day did not consent to follow your will…
work: Words to the captive King John II of France at supper, 1356 (Froissart, Chronicles)
note: Froissart's account

speaker: john-stuart-mill
text: The only freedom which deserves the name, is that of pursuing our own good in our own way, so long as we do not attempt to deprive others of theirs, or impede their efforts to obtain it.
work: On Liberty (1859), ch. 1

speaker: pandita-ramabai
text: After many years of careful observation and thought, I have come to the conclusion that the chief needs of high-caste Hindu women are:– 1st, Self-Reliance; 2nd, Education; 3rd, Native Women Teachers.
work: The High-Caste Hindu Woman (1887)

speaker: james-madison
text: The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands, whether of one, a few, or many, and whether hereditary, self-appointed, or elective, may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.
work: The Federalist No. 47 (1788)
note: published under the name Publius

speaker: gyges-of-lydia
text: Our fathers, in time past, distinguished right and wrong plainly enough, and it is our wisdom to submit to be taught by them.
work: Refusing the king Candaules, who wished him to see the queen unclothed (Herodotus, Histories, book 1)
note: Herodotus's account
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: bohemond-i-of-antioch
text: Seignors, take heed all of you, for we are pilgrims of God. We ought, therefore, to be better and more humble than before. Do not plunder this land, since it belongs to Christians…
work: Words to his army on its march through the Balkans, 1096 (Gesta Francorum)
note: as the anonymous Gesta Francorum, written by a knight in his following about 1100, records them

speaker: john-knox
text: God forbid, that ever I take upon me to command any to obey me, or yet to set subjects at liberty to do what pleaseth them. But my travail is that both princes and subjects obey God.
work: History of the Reformation in Scotland, book 4 (modernized edition, 1905)
note: his own account of his interview with Mary, Queen of Scots, 1561

speaker: john-adams
text: It seems to be the intention of Heaven that we should be taught the full value of our liberty by the dearness of the purchase, and the importance of public virtue by the necessity of it.
work: Letter to Abigail Adams from Passy, 1778

speaker: arthur-conan-doyle
text: It has long been an axiom of mine that the little things are infinitely the most important.
work: A Case of Identity (1891)
note: spoken by Sherlock Holmes

speaker: theocritus
text: On shadowy boughs the burnt cicalas kept their chattering toil, far off the little owl cried in the thick thorn brake, the larks and finches were singing, the ring-dove moaned, the yellow bees were flitting about the springs.
work: Idylls, 7 (The Harvest Feast)

speaker: enrico-dandolo
text: I am a man old and feeble, who should have need of rest, and I am sick in body; but I see that no one could command and lead you like myself, who am your lord.
work: Speech in St Mark's, Venice, 1202 (Villehardouin, The Conquest of Constantinople)
note: Villehardouin's account; he was there; the doge was blind and very old

speaker: robert-schumann
text: Endeavour to play easy pieces well and with elegance; that is better than to play difficult pieces badly.
work: Advice to Young Musicians (1850)

speaker: booker-t-washington
text: In all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress.
work: Address at the Atlanta Cotton States Exposition, 1895 (Up from Slavery, chapter 14)

speaker: samuel-de-champlain
text: One might judge, if the territory four leagues in extent lying between Panama and this river were cut through, he could pass from the south sea to that on the other side, and thus shorten the route by more than fifteen hundred leagues.
work: Brief Discours, on the Isthmus of Panama (c. 1601)
credit: tr. in the Prince Society edition of his Voyages, 1880

speaker: cao-pi
text: Alas that I was born in these times, To be blown along like a cloud puffed by the wind!
work: He abandons the campaign

speaker: chretien-de-troyes
text: The rustic's proverb says that many a thing is despised that is worth much more than is supposed.
work: Erec and Enide, opening lines

speaker: george-washington-williams
text: Not as the blind panegyrist of my race, nor as the partisan apologist, but from a love for "the truth of history," I have striven to record the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.
work: History of the Negro Race in America from 1619 to 1880 (1883), preface

speaker: william-pitt-the-elder
text: I rejoice that America has resisted. Three millions of people, so dead to all the feelings of liberty as voluntarily to submit to be slaves, would have been fit instruments to make slaves of the rest.
work: Speech in the House of Commons on the Stamp Act, 14 January 1766
note: as the parliamentary reports reconstructed it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: machado-de-assis
text: The truth unknown to man is the madness of him who proclaims it.
work: Life (1886), a dialogue in Brazilian Tales
note: spoken by Prometheus to Ahasverus, the Wandering Jew

speaker: aristippus-of-cyrene
text: …it is not those who know a great many things, but they who know what is useful who are valuable men.
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 2
note: to a man proud of the variety of his learning

speaker: wolfram-von-eschenbach
text: And shaming alike and honour are his who such doubt shall show, For it standeth in evil contrast with a true man's dauntless might, As one seeth the magpie's plumage, which at one while is black and white.
work: Parzival, opening lines
note: of the man of wavering faith, likened to a magpie's plumage

speaker: william-bradford-governor
text: …they fell upon their knees and blessed the God of Heaven who had brought them over the vast and furious ocean…
work: Of Plymouth Plantation, on the landfall at Cape Cod, 1620
note: in Harold Paget's modern spelling (1909)

speaker: mark-twain
text: Truth is stranger than fiction, but it is because Fiction is obliged to stick to possibilities; Truth isn’t.
work: Following the Equator (1897), chapter 15
note: a motto from "Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar"

speaker: josephus
text: Now he is equally a coward who will not die when he is obliged to die, and he who will die when he is not obliged so to do.
work: To his companions in the cave at Jotapata, 67 (The Jewish War, book 3)
note: his own account

speaker: marie-de-france
text: But this is the way of the world, that when a man or woman sings more tunably than his fellows, those about the fire fall upon him, pell-mell, for reason of their envy.
work: The Lay of Gugemar, prologue
note: on envious listeners

speaker: pu-songling
text: Alas! I am but the bird that, dreading the winter frost, finds no shelter in the tree: the autumn insect that chirps to the moon, and hugs the door for warmth.
work: Strange Stories from a Chinese Studio (1679), the author's own record

speaker: william-tecumseh-sherman
text: I beg to present you as a Christmas-gift the city of Savannah, with one hundred and fifty heavy guns and plenty of ammunition, also about twenty five thousand bales of cotton.
work: Telegram to President Lincoln, 22 December 1864 (Memoirs, 1875)

speaker: scipio-africanus
text: The man who by temperance has curbed and subdued his appetite for them, has acquired for himself much greater honour and a much more important victory than we now enjoy in the conquest of Syphax.
work: Speech to Masinissa (Livy, History of Rome, book 30)
note: Livy's account

speaker: thomas-cranmer
text: That you set not your minds overmuch upon this deceitful world, but upon God, and upon the world to come…
work: His last exhortation before his burning, Oxford, 21 March 1556
note: as Foxe recorded it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: patrick-henry
text: The battle, sir, is not to the strong alone; it is to the vigilant, the active, the brave.
work: Speech to the Second Virginia Convention, 1775
note: as William Wirt reconstructed it (1817)

speaker: william-morris
text: Yes, surely! and if others can see it as I have seen it, then it may be called a vision rather than a dream.
work: News from Nowhere (1890), closing words

speaker: jesus
text: It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God.
work: Matthew 19:24, to his disciples after the rich young man went away
note: as Matthew's Gospel records it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: olaf-tryggvason
text: Why do ye strike so gently that ye seldom cut?
work: Words at the battle of Svolder, 1000 (Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Saga of Olaf Trygvason)
note: Snorri Sturluson's account, written two centuries later

speaker: tiberius
text: Let them hate me, so long as they do but approve my conduct.
work: Suetonius, Life of Tiberius, 59
credit: tr. Alexander Thomson, 1796, rev. T. Forester
note: of the verses written against him; Suetonius' account

speaker: walter-bagehot
text: The efficient secret of the English Constitution may be described as the close union, the nearly complete fusion, of the executive and legislative powers.
work: The English Constitution (1867), ch. 1, The Cabinet

speaker: ludvig-holberg
text: Folks in the village say that Jeppe drinks, but they don't say why Jeppe drinks…
work: Jeppe of the Hill (1722), act 1
credit: tr. Oscar James Campbell and Frederic Schenck, 1914
note: spoken by the peasant Jeppe

speaker: belisarius
text: …we on our side permit the Goths to have the whole of Britain, which is much larger than Sicily and was subject to the Romans in early times.
work: Reply to the Gothic envoys during the siege of Rome, 537 (Procopius, History of the Wars, book 6, chapter 6)
note: Procopius' account; the Goths had offered to give up Sicily

speaker: olaf-ii-of-norway
text: Thou art a very lucky man, Sigvat; but it is not wonderful that luck should accompany understanding. It is only wonderful how it sometimes happens that luck attends ignorant men, and that foolish counsel turns out lucky.
work: Words to the skald Sigvat (Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Saga of Olaf Haraldson)
note: Snorri Sturluson's account; Sigvat had named the king's newborn son Magnus without leave

speaker: seneca-the-younger
text: The greatest remedy for anger is delay: beg anger to grant you this at the first, not in order that it may pardon the offence, but that it may form a right judgment about it: if it delays, it will come to an end.
work: On Anger, book 2, 29

speaker: lope-de-vega
text: But what can I do if I have written four hundred and eighty-three comedies, along with one which I have finished this week? For all of these, except six, gravely sin against art.
work: The New Art of Writing Plays (1609)

speaker: ernest-renan
text: I am double, as it were, and one half of me laughs while the other weeps. This is the explanation of my cheerfulness. As I am two spirits in one body, one of them has always cause to be content.
work: Recollections of My Youth (1883)

speaker: henry-viii-of-england
text: I send you, by the bearer of this, a buck killed late last night by my own hand, hoping that when you eat of it you may think of the hunter…
work: Letter to Anne Boleyn, c. 1527
credit: translated from his French (translator not named)

speaker: multatuli
text: …it is a fact that famine is often the consequence of these measures; but the flags of the ships, laden with the harvest that makes Holland rich, are flapping gaily at Batavia…
work: Max Havelaar (1860), on the cultivation system in Java

speaker: isidore-of-seville
text: Philosophy is the knowledge of things human and divine, united with a zeal for right living.
work: Etymologies, book 2

speaker: rabbi-akiva
text: Everything is foreseen, yet free will is given…
work: Sayings of the Fathers (Pirke Avot) 3:19
note: as the Mishnah records his saying

speaker: william-pitt-the-younger
text: I know that the interests of the two Countries must be taken together, and that a man cannot speak as a true Englishman, unless he speaks as a true Irishman, nor as a true Irishman, unless he speaks as a true Englishman…
work: Speech in the House of Commons on union with Ireland, 31 January 1799

speaker: elizabeth-cady-stanton
text: I soon convinced Miss Anthony that the ballot was the key to the situation; that when we had a voice in the laws we should be welcome to any platform.
work: Eighty Years and More (1898), on her friendship with Susan B. Anthony

speaker: john-the-baptist
text: He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise.
work: Luke 3:11, answering the people who asked what they should do
note: as Luke's Gospel records it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: pedro-calderon-de-la-barca
text: In this world's uncertain gleam, That to live is but to dream: Man dreams what he is, and wakes Only when upon him breaks Death's mysterious morning beam.
work: Life Is a Dream (1635), act 2
note: spoken by Prince Sigismund

speaker: theodor-herzl
text: No one can deny the gravity of the situation of the Jews. Wherever they live in perceptible numbers, they are more or less persecuted.
work: The Jewish State (1896), ch. 2
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: saxo-grammaticus
text: …since this present work promises not a trumpery dazzle of language, but faithful information concerning times past.
work: Gesta Danorum (The Danish History), preface

speaker: mary-wollstonecraft
text: But, if women are to be excluded, without having a voice, from a participation of the natural rights of mankind, prove first, to ward off the charge of injustice and inconsistency, that they want reason…
work: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), dedication to Talleyrand

speaker: mary-mother-of-jesus
text: He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.
work: The Magnificat, Luke 1:52
note: her song as Luke's Gospel gives it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: w-b-yeats
text: How many loved your moments of glad grace, And loved your beauty will love false or true; But one man loved the pilgrim soul in you, And loved the sorrows of your changing face.
work: When You Are Old (1892)

speaker: ibn-tufayl
text: And when he perceiv'd that his Island was encompass'd by the Sea, he thought that there was no other Land in the World but only that Island.
work: Hayy ibn Yaqzan
note: of his hero Hayy, growing up alone on the island

speaker: johann-wolfgang-von-goethe
text: The wild desires no longer win us, The deeds of passion cease to chain; The love of Man revives within us, The love of God revives again.
work: Faust, part 1 (1808), the Study
note: spoken by Faust

speaker: bias-of-priene
text: Hold your tongues, lest they should find out that you are in this ship.
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 1
note: to impious sailors who began praying to the gods in a storm

speaker: roger-williams
text: It is the will and command of God that, since the coming of his Son the Lord Jesus, a permission of the most Paganish, Jewish, Turkish, or anti-christian consciences and worships be granted to all men in all nations and countries…
work: The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution for Cause of Conscience (1644), preface
note: in the modernised spelling of the 1848 Hanserd Knollys Society edition

speaker: winston-churchill
text: The representatives of every Colony have expressed the opinion that the worst they saw here, was the extreme of poverty side by side with the extreme of luxury.
work: Liberalism and the Social Problem (1909), speeches

speaker: phocion
text: For as for myself, to have it in my power to sacrifice my own life and fortune for the common safety, I should think the greatest of good fortune.
work: Plutarch, Life of Phocion
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: when Alexander demanded that Athens hand over its leaders; Plutarch's account

speaker: murasaki-shikibu
text: I see that I have been slighted, hated, and looked down upon as an old gossip, and I must bear it, for it is my destiny to be solitary.
work: Diary, 1008-1010 (in Diaries of Court Ladies of Old Japan)
credit: tr. Annie Shepley Omori and Kochi Doi, 1920

speaker: marcus-junius-brutus
text: The Xanthians, suspecting my kindness, have made their country the grave of their despair; the Patareans, trusting themselves to me, enjoy in all points their former liberty; it is in your power to choose the judgment of the Patareans or the fortune of the Xanthians.
work: Plutarch, Life of Brutus
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: a letter to the city of Patara, after the people of Xanthus had destroyed themselves rather than yield to him; Plutarch's account

speaker: ramon-llull
text: I am alone, now that I have seen you and heard you; until now, I was in the company of my Beloved.
work: The Book of the Lover and the Beloved, verse 46 (from Blanquerna, about 1283)
note: the Lover's answer to passers-by who asked why he sat alone

speaker: cesare-beccaria
text: …the history of mankind conveys to us the idea of an immense sea of errors, among which a few truths, confusedly and at long intervals, float on the surface.
work: On Crimes and Punishments (1764), chapter 28

speaker: soren-kierkegaard
text: My melancholy is the most faithful sweetheart I have had—no wonder that I return the love!
work: Either/Or (1843), Diapsalmata
note: from the Diapsalmata, written in the voice of the pseudonymous aesthete "A"

speaker: alcibiades
text: …we have reached a position in which we must not be content with retaining but must scheme to extend it, for, if we cease to rule others, we are in danger of being ruled ourselves.
work: Speech for the Sicilian expedition (Thucydides, book 6)
note: Thucydides' account

speaker: shinran
text: When every man is beloved of us, even as the son of our own body, there is the Universal Mind made perfect in us.
work: Wasan (hymns), 90
credit: tr. S. Yamabe and L. Adams Beck, 1921

speaker: mikhail-bakunin
text: I receive and I give—such is human life. Each directs and is directed in his turn. Therefore there is no fixed and constant authority, but a continual exchange of mutual, temporary, and, above all, voluntary authority and subordination.
work: God and the State (written 1871)

speaker: daniel-defoe
text: I learned to look more upon the bright side of my condition, and less upon the dark side, and to consider what I enjoyed rather than what I wanted…
work: Robinson Crusoe (1719)
note: narrated by Robinson Crusoe

speaker: tomyris
text: …cease to do so, I say, and be king over thine own people, and endure to see us ruling those whom we rule.
work: Herodotus, Histories, book 1 (message to Cyrus as he bridged the river into her land)
note: Herodotus' account

speaker: pope-urban-ii
text: Short is the way, little the labor, which, nevertheless, will repay you with the crown that fadeth not away.
work: Speech at the Council of Clermont, 1095 (Balderic of Dol's version)
note: the speech as Balderic of Dol retold it some years later

speaker: robert-louis-stevenson
text: Give us courage and gaiety and the quiet mind. Spare to us our friends, soften to us our enemies.
work: Prayers Written at Vailima, Samoa (1904)

speaker: gottfried-wilhelm-leibniz
text: Thus the organic body of each living being is a kind of divine machine or natural automaton, which infinitely surpasses all artificial automata.
work: Monadology (1714), section 64
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: alp-arslan
text: …the earth seemed to tremble under my feet; and I said in my heart, Surely thou art the king of the world, the greatest and most invincible of warriors.
work: His dying words, 1072 (in Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 57)
note: as Gibbon gives them from the Persian historians

speaker: david-lloyd-george
text: Peace is only possible when you introduce into the attitude of nations towards each other principles which govern the demeanour of decent people in a community towards their neighbours.
work: Where Are We Going? (1923)

speaker: hezekiah
text: The living, the living, he shall praise thee, as I do this day: the father to the children shall make known thy truth.
work: Isaiah 38:19, his song on recovering from sickness
note: the writing the Book of Isaiah gives as his
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: cyrus-the-younger
text: On the whole my fear is, not that I may not have enough to give to each of my friends, but lest I may not have friends enough on whom to bestow what I have to give…
work: To his Greek officers before the battle of Cunaxa, 401 BCE (Xenophon, Anabasis, book 1)
note: Xenophon's account; he was marching to take the throne from his brother

speaker: marquis-de-lafayette
text: I am still floating on this dreary plain, the most wearisome of all human habitations.
work: Letter to his wife from the Atlantic crossing, 1777
credit: tr. 1837, in the edition published by his family (translator not named)

speaker: michelangelo
text: My beard turns up to heaven; my nape falls in, Fixed on my spine: my breast-bone visibly Grows like a harp: a rich embroidery Bedews my face from brush-drops thick and thin.
work: Sonnet to Giovanni da Pistoia, on painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling

speaker: yung-wing
text: The more one knows, the more he suffers and is consequently less happy; the less one knows, the less he suffers, and hence is more happy.
work: My Life in China and America (1909), ch. 5

speaker: otho
text: Believe it many times over, I can die with more honor than I can reign.
work: Plutarch, Life of Otho
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: to his soldiers after the defeat at Bedriacum, 69 CE; Plutarch's account

speaker: agesilaus-ii
text: I don’t think that shoemaker a good workman that makes a great shoe for a little foot.
work: Plutarch, Sayings of the Spartans (Moralia)
credit: tr. several hands, rev. William W. Goodwin, 1870
note: to one who praised an orator for making much of small matters; Plutarch's collection of sayings

speaker: william-caxton
text: And for to pass the time this book shall be pleasant to read in; but for to give faith and believe that all is true that is contained herein, ye be at your liberty.
work: Preface to Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur (1485)
note: in modernised spelling

speaker: henry-wadsworth-longfellow
text: Ships that pass in the night, and speak each other in passing, Only a signal shown and a distant voice in the darkness; So on the ocean of life we pass and speak one another…
work: Tales of a Wayside Inn, part 3 (1873), the Theologian's tale

speaker: adam-ferguson
text: Mankind are to be taken in groupes, as they have always subsisted. The history of the individual is but a detail of the sentiments and the thoughts he has entertained in the view of his species…
work: An Essay on the History of Civil Society (1767), part 1

speaker: lucius-aemilius-paullus-macedonicus
text: …since she has sufficiently wreaked her jealousy at our great successes on me and mine, and has made the conqueror as marked an example of human instability as the captive whom he led in triumph…
work: Plutarch, Life of Aemilius Paulus
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: of Fortune, after losing two sons in the days of his triumph; Plutarch's account

speaker: teresa-of-avila
text: It is like a dying man with the candle in his hand, on the point of dying the death desired.
work: The Life of St. Teresa, chapter 16
note: of the prayer of union, the third water of the soul's garden

speaker: polybius
text: …to keep well in mind in the midst of prosperity the mutability of Fortune, is the characteristic of a great man…
work: Histories, book 38
note: of Scipio Aemilianus at the fall of Carthage

speaker: anselm-of-canterbury
text: Enter the inner chamber of your mind; shut out all thoughts save that of God, and such as can aid you in seeking him; close your door and seek him.
work: Proslogion, chapter 1

speaker: vincent-van-gogh
text: A violet city, yellow stars, a green-blue sky, crops of all colours, old-gold, copper, green-gold, red-gold, yellow-gold, yellow-bronze, green and red. I painted it in the midst of a North wind.
work: Letter from Arles, 1888 (The Letters of a Post-Impressionist)

speaker: attila
text: For what is war but your usual custom? Or what is sweeter for a brave man than to seek revenge with his own hand?
work: Speech before the battle of the Catalaunian Plains, 451 (Jordanes, Getica, 39)
note: Jordanes' account, written a century later

speaker: chretien-de-troyes
text: For lovers used to deserve to be considered courteous, brave, generous, and honourable. But now love is a laughing-stock, for those who have no intelligence of it assert that they love, and in that they lie.
work: Yvain, or the Knight with the Lion, opening lines
note: on the decline of love since King Arthur's day

speaker: christopher-marlowe
text: Doth teach us all to have aspiring minds: Our souls, whose faculties can comprehend The wondrous architecture of the world, And measure every wandering planet's course, Still climbing after knowledge infinite, And always moving as the restless spheres…
work: Tamburlaine the Great, part 1 (c. 1587), act 2
note: spoken by Tamburlaine

speaker: croesus
text: Thy subjects, the Persians, are a poor people with a proud spirit. If then thou lettest them pillage and possess themselves of great wealth, I will tell thee what thou hast to expect at their hands.
work: Counsel to Cyrus as the Persians plundered Sardis (Herodotus, Histories, book 1)
note: Herodotus's account
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: heinrich-schliemann
text: These are, however, an irrefragable proof that the Treasure belongs to the city and to the age of which Homer sings.
work: Troy and Its Remains (1875), on the treasure he called Priam's

speaker: ben-jonson
text: I loved the man, and do honour his memory on this side idolatry as much as any.
work: Timber, or Discoveries (1641), on Shakespeare

speaker: bayezid-i
text: By the divine clemency, our invincible cimeter has reduced to our obedience almost all Asia, with many and large countries in Europe, excepting only the city of Constantinople; for beyond the walls thou hast nothing left.
work: Letter to the emperor Manuel II (in Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 64)
note: as Gibbon gives it

speaker: calgacus
text: Fear and terror there certainly are, feeble bonds of attachment; remove them, and those who have ceased to fear will begin to hate.
work: Speech before the battle of Mons Graupius (Tacitus, Agricola, 32)
credit: tr. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb, 1877
note: Tacitus' account

speaker: john-redmond
text: Why do not these English statesmen give us something to be loyal to? What claim has such a system as that to loyalty?
work: Speech on the coronation of Edward VII, 1902
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: ethan-allen
text: The sun seemed to rise that morning with a superior lustre; and Ticonderoga and its dependencies smiled on its conquerors…
work: Narrative of his captivity (1779), the morning after the capture of Fort Ticonderoga

speaker: xerxes-i
text: Success for the most part attends those who act boldly, not those who weigh everything, and are slack to venture.
work: To his uncle Artabanus at Abydos, 480 BCE (Herodotus, Histories, book 7)
note: Herodotus's account
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: caratacus
text: My punishment would be followed by oblivion, whereas, if you save my life, I shall be an everlasting memorial of your clemency.
work: Speech before Claudius in Rome, 51 CE (Tacitus, Annals, book 12)
credit: tr. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb, 1876
note: Tacitus' account

speaker: olaf-iii-of-norway
text: In the days of my father these people were subjected to much terror and fear; the most of them concealed their gold and their precious things, but now I see glittering on his person what each one owns, and your freedom is my gladness.
work: Words at a guild feast (Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Saga of Olaf Kyrre)
note: Snorri Sturluson's account; the son of Harald Hardrada, he was called Olaf the Peaceful

speaker: karl-marx
text: The tradition of all past generations weighs like an alp upon the brain of the living.
work: The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte (1852), ch. 1

speaker: john-pym
text: The greatest liberty of the kingdom is religion; thereby we are freed from spiritual evils, and no impositions are so grievous as those that are laid upon the soul.
work: Speech in the House of Commons on grievances, April 1640
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: cnut-the-great
text: …that they by no means, either through fear of myself, or favour to any powerful person, suffer, henceforth, any injustice, or cause such, to be done in all my kingdom.
work: Letter to the English from Rome, 1027 (William of Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England, book 2)
credit: tr. John Sharpe, 1815, revised by J. A. Giles, 1847
note: the letter as William of Malmesbury copied it a century later; to his counsellors

speaker: pope-gregory-vii
text: …he presented himself at the gate of the castle, barefoot and clad only in wretched woollen garments, beseeching us with tears to grant him absolution and forgiveness. This he continued to do for three days…
work: Letter to the German princes on the penance at Canossa, January 1077
credit: tr. Oliver J. Thatcher and Edgar H. McNeal, 1905
note: of King Henry IV

speaker: plautus
text: Doubtless we all are free men more willingly than we live the life of slaves.
work: The Captives (Captivi)
note: spoken by a captive in the play

speaker: emir-abdelkader
text: Vice is condemned in all religions; and to allow oneself to be carried away by it is like taking a poisonous aliment into the stomach.
work: Letter to Imam Shamil, 1860
note: from Churchill's Life of Abdel Kader

speaker: isaac-watts
text: Joy to the world; the Lord is come; Let earth receive her King; Let every heart prepare him room, And heaven and nature sing.
work: Psalm 98, The Psalms of David Imitated (1719)

speaker: pope-innocent-iii
text: We decree that no Christian shall use violence to compel the Jews to accept baptism.
work: Decree on the Jews (Constitutio pro Judeis), 1199
credit: tr. Oliver J. Thatcher and Edgar H. McNeal, 1905

speaker: booker-t-washington
text: The opportunity to earn a dollar in a factory just now is worth infinitely more than the opportunity to spend a dollar in an opera-house.
work: Address at the Atlanta Cotton States Exposition, 1895 (Up from Slavery, chapter 14)

speaker: plotinus
text: Remove from your soul, therefore, all that is superfluous, straighten out all that is crooked, purify and illuminate what is obscure, and do not cease perfecting your statue until the divine resplendence of virtue shines forth upon your sight…
work: Enneads, 1.6 (Of Beauty), 9

speaker: william-bradford-governor
text: …they now had no friends to welcome them, nor inns to entertain and refresh their weather-beaten bodies, nor houses—much less towns—to repair to.
work: Of Plymouth Plantation, on the landfall at Cape Cod, 1620
note: in Harold Paget's modern spelling (1909)

speaker: saint-cuthbert
text: Let concord be mutual between you and other servants of Christ; and do not despise others who belong to the faith and come to you for hospitality, but admit them familiarly and kindly…
work: His last words to the monks of Lindisfarne, 687 (Bede, Life of St. Cuthbert, chapter 39)
note: as the abbot Herefrith, who was with him, told them to Bede

speaker: leonidas-i
text: If you esteem number, all Greece is not able to match a small part of that army; if courage, this number is sufficient.
work: Plutarch, Sayings of the Spartans (Moralia)
credit: tr. several hands, rev. William W. Goodwin, 1870
note: asked how he could fight so great a number with so few; Plutarch's collection of sayings

speaker: fyodor-dostoevsky
text: Is it true, prince, that you once declared that ‘beauty would save the world’?
work: The Idiot (1869), part 3
note: spoken by Ippolit to Prince Myshkin

speaker: josephus
text: The bodies of all men are indeed mortal, and are created out of corruptible matter; but the soul is ever immortal, and is a portion of the divinity that inhabits our bodies.
work: To his companions in the cave at Jotapata, 67 (The Jewish War, book 3)
note: his own account

speaker: john-marshall
text: Let the end be legitimate, let it be within the scope of the Constitution, and all means which are appropriate, which are plainly adapted to that end, which are not prohibited, but consist with the letter and spirit of the Constitution, are Constitutional.
work: Opinion of the Court, McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: hrotsvitha-of-gandersheim
text: I strive only, although my power is not equal to my desire, to use what talent I have for the glory of Him Who gave it me.
work: Preface to her plays
note: on taking the Roman playwright Terence as her model

speaker: mark-twain
text: Man is the Only Animal that Blushes. Or needs to.
work: Following the Equator (1897), chapter 27
note: a motto from "Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar"

speaker: jesus
text: Render therefore unto Cesar the things which are Cesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
work: Matthew 22:21, asked whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar
note: as Matthew's Gospel records it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: aphra-behn
text: …if they died in the Attempt, it would be more brave, than to live in perpetual Slavery.
work: Oroonoko, or The Royal Slave (1688)
note: the narrator reporting Oroonoko's speech to his fellow captives

speaker: joseph-conrad
text: The way is to the destructive element submit yourself, and with the exertions of your hands and feet in the water make the deep, deep sea keep you up.
work: Lord Jim (1900), ch. 20
note: spoken by Stein

speaker: sei-shonagon
text: But for my part, even if they come very late and very drunk, I absolutely refuse to give them even so much as a bowl of rice.
work: The Pillow-Book, on gentlemen who expect to be fed in the ladies' rooms

speaker: david
text: Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
work: Psalm 23:4
note: from a psalm the Bible heads "A Psalm of David"
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: francisco-de-quevedo
text: I told her, that I had seen it in the corruption and avarice of wicked magistrates; in the pride and haughtiness of grandees; in the appetites of the voluptuous…
work: The Visions (1627), the Vision of Death
note: the narrator, telling Death where he had seen hell before

speaker: henrik-ibsen
text: But our home has been nothing but a playroom. I have been your doll-wife, just as at home I was papa’s doll-child; and here the children have been my dolls.
work: A Doll's House (1879), act 3
note: spoken by Nora

speaker: isaiah
text: Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!
work: Isaiah 5:20
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: edward-the-black-prince
text: …methinks ye ought to rejoice, though the journey be not as ye would have had it, for this day ye have won the high renown of prowess and have passed this day in valiantness all other of your party.
work: Words to the captive King John II of France at supper, 1356 (Froissart, Chronicles)
note: Froissart's account

speaker: lord-byron
text: I have not loved the world, nor the world me; I have not flattered its rank breath, nor bowed To its idolatries a patient knee…
work: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, canto 3 (1816)

speaker: mary-shelley
text: Life, although it may only be an accumulation of anguish, is dear to me, and I will defend it.
work: Frankenstein (1818), ch. 10
note: spoken by the creature to his maker

speaker: bertrand-russell
text: The glorification of the State, and the doctrine that it is every citizen's duty to serve the State, are radically against progress and against liberty.
work: Proposed Roads to Freedom (1918), ch. 5

speaker: nehemiah
text: Should such a man as I flee? and who is there, that, being as I am, would go into the temple to save his life? I will not go in.
work: Nehemiah 6:11, urged to hide in the Temple from those who plotted against him
note: his own memoir as the Book of Nehemiah gives it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: abd-al-rahman-iii
text: I have now reigned above fifty years in victory or peace; beloved by my subjects, dreaded by my enemies, and respected by my allies.
work: Memorial found among his papers after his death, 961 (Gibbon, Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, chapter 52)
note: as Edward Gibbon renders it from the Arabic historians through Cardonne's French

speaker: daniel-oconnell
text: Yes, my friends, the Union was begot in iniquity—it was perpetuated in fraud and cruelty. It was no compact, no bargain, but it was an act of the most decided tyranny and corruption that was ever yet perpetrated.
work: Speech at the Mullaghmast meeting, 1843
note: on the Act of Union of 1800
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: lajos-kossuth
text: So long as despots exist, and have the means to pay, they will find men to calumniate those who are opposed to tyranny.
work: Select Speeches of Kossuth (1854), in America, 1851-52
note: spoken in English, in exile after the Hungarian revolution

speaker: alphonse-de-lamartine
text: The French Revolution was therefore in its essence a sublime and impassioned spirituality.
work: History of the Girondists (1847), book 1

speaker: elijah
text: It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.
work: 1 Kings 19:4, fleeing into the wilderness
note: as the First Book of Kings tells it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: alcuin-of-york
text: It is now nearly 350 years that we and our fathers have dwelt in this most fair land, and never before has such a horror appeared in Britain as we now have suffered at the hands of pagans.
work: Letter to King Ethelred of Northumbria on the sack of Lindisfarne, 793

speaker: john-knox
text: If their princes exceed their bounds, Madam, no doubt they should be resisted, even by power.
work: History of the Reformation in Scotland, book 4 (modernized edition, 1905)
note: his own account of his interview with Mary, Queen of Scots, 1561

speaker: arthur-conan-doyle
text: …life is infinitely stranger than anything which the mind of man could invent. We would not dare to conceive the things which are really mere commonplaces of existence.
work: A Case of Identity (1891)
note: spoken by Sherlock Holmes

speaker: ahab
text: Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?
work: 1 Kings 21:20, meeting the prophet Elijah in Naboth's vineyard
note: as the First Book of Kings tells it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: william-pitt-the-elder
text: My Lord, I am sure I can save this country, and no one else can.
work: To the Duke of Devonshire, 1756
note: as Horace Walpole recorded it in his memoirs

speaker: ramon-llull
text: Whether Lover and Beloved are near or far is all one; for their love mingles as water mingles with wine. They are linked as heat with light; they approach and are united as Essence and Being.
work: The Book of the Lover and the Beloved, verse 49 (from Blanquerna, about 1283)

speaker: machado-de-assis
text: I never labored. Labor is a refuge, and that refuge was denied me.
work: Life (1886), a dialogue in Brazilian Tales
note: spoken by Ahasverus, the Wandering Jew

speaker: marie-de-france
text: But should rough hands part so fond a clasping, the hazel would wither at the root, and the honeysuckle must fail. Fair friend, thus is the case with us, nor you without me, nor I without you.
work: The Lay of the Honeysuckle (Chevrefoil)
note: of the lay's lovers, Tristan and Isolde, likened to the honeysuckle and the hazel

speaker: pu-songling
text: As it is, midnight finds me with an expiring lamp, while the wind whistles mournfully without; and over my cheerless table I piece together my tales…
work: Strange Stories from a Chinese Studio (1679), the author's own record

speaker: jezebel
text: Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?
work: 2 Kings 9:31, from her window, as Jehu came through the gate
note: as the Second Book of Kings tells it; Zimri had killed his king and reigned seven days
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: benjamin-disraeli
text: I do not know that; even Napoleon regretted that he had ever re-crossed the Mediterranean. The East is a career.
work: Tancred (1847)
note: spoken by Sidonia

speaker: oliver-cromwell
text: What I judge to be the end of your meeting, the great end, which was likewise remembered to you this day; to wit, is healing and settling.
work: Speech at the opening of the first Protectorate Parliament, 4 September 1654
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: cornplanter
text: When you kindled your thirteen fires separately, the wise men that assembled at them told us that you were all brothers, the children of one great father…
work: Speech to President Washington, Philadelphia, 1790
note: as printed in John Niles Hubbard's account of Red Jacket (1886)

speaker: sappho
text: As on the hills the shepherds trample the hyacinth under foot, and the flower darkens on the ground.
work: Fragments

speaker: henry-iv-holy-roman-emperor
text: Come down, come down, and be accursed through all the ages.
work: Letter to Pope Gregory VII, January 1076, the closing words
credit: tr. Oliver J. Thatcher and Edgar H. McNeal, 1905
note: written for the synod of Worms that declared the pope deposed

speaker: peter-kropotkin
text: But what right had I to these higher joys, when all round me was nothing but misery and struggle for a mouldy bit of bread…
work: Memoirs of a Revolutionist (1899), part 4
note: on giving up geography for the revolutionary cause

speaker: sojourner-truth
text: The Lord only knows how many times I let my children go hungry, rather than take secretly the bread I liked not to ask for.
work: The Narrative of Sojourner Truth (1850), on her years in slavery
note: as told to Olive Gilbert, who wrote the Narrative

speaker: ludvig-holberg
text: It is all one to me, too, what the bailiff or the others here in the village think on the subject; for I know that the earth is round.
work: Erasmus Montanus (1723), act 3
credit: tr. Oscar James Campbell and Frederic Schenck, 1914
note: spoken by the student Montanus to the villagers

speaker: snorri-sturluson
text: But the songs seem to me most reliable if they are sung correctly, and judiciously interpreted.
work: Heimskringla, preface
note: on the skalds' poems as sources for the kings' lives

speaker: seneca-the-younger
text: A large part of mankind manufacture their own grievances either by entertaining unfounded suspicions or by exaggerating trifles. Anger often comes to us, but we often go to it.
work: On Anger, book 3, 12

speaker: hans-christian-andersen
text: Madame, politics are like Venus; they whom she decoys into her castle perish.
work: The True Story of My Life (1847)

speaker: david-hume
text: It is not contrary to reason to prefer the destruction of the whole world to the scratching of my finger.
work: A Treatise of Human Nature, book 2, part 3, section 3

speaker: harald-hardrada
text: Let us now fall upon some good sensible counsel; for it is not to be concealed that this is an hostile army and the king himself without doubt is here.
work: Words at Stamford Bridge, 1066, on sighting the English army (Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Saga of Harald Hardrade)
note: Snorri Sturluson's account, written a century and a half later

speaker: samuel-johnson
text: No man but a blockhead ever wrote, except for money.
work: In conversation, 5 April 1776 (Boswell, Life of Johnson)
note: Boswell's account

speaker: xenophanes
text: The gods have not revealed all things to men from the beginning, but by seeking they find in time what is better.
work: Fragments (Burnet 16)

speaker: frederick-douglass
text: A man, without force, is without the essential dignity of humanity. Human nature is so constituted, that it cannot honor a helpless man, although it can pity him…
work: My Bondage and My Freedom (1855), on his fight with the slave-breaker Covey

speaker: prince-shotoku
text: Good faith is the foundation of right. In everything let there be good faith, for in it there surely consists the good and the bad, success and failure.
work: Seventeen-Article Constitution, 604, article 9 (Nihongi, book 22)
note: the constitution the Nihongi attributes to him
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: maimonides
text: …the plain meaning must be as valuable as silver, and the hidden meaning still more precious; so that the figurative meaning bears the same relation to the literal one as gold to silver.
work: The Guide for the Perplexed, introduction
note: on the figures of the prophets, after Proverbs' apples of gold in settings of silver

speaker: ludwig-van-beethoven
text: When I open my eyes, a sigh involuntarily escapes me, for all that I see runs counter to my religion; perforce I despise the world which does not intuitively feel that music is a higher revelation than all wisdom and philosophy.
work: Reported by Bettina von Arnim, 1810 (Beethoven: the Man and the Artist, as Revealed in His Own Words)
note: as Bettina von Arnim reported his words in a letter to Goethe

speaker: empedocles
text: Friends, that inhabit the great town looking down on the yellow rock of Akragas, up by the citadel, busy in goodly works, harbours of honour for the stranger, men unskilled in meanness, all hail. I go about among you an immortal god, no mortal now…
work: Purifications, opening (Burnet 112)
note: addressed to the people of his city, Akragas

speaker: w-e-b-du-bois
text: He would not Africanize America, for America has too much to teach the world and Africa. He would not bleach his Negro soul in a flood of white Americanism, for he knows that Negro blood has a message for the world.
work: The Souls of Black Folk (1903), chapter 1

speaker: saxo-grammaticus
text: So he chose to feign dulness, and pretend an utter lack of wits. This cunning course not only concealed his intelligence but ensured his safety.
work: Gesta Danorum (The Danish History), book 3
note: of the Danish prince Amleth, whose story Shakespeare's Hamlet retells

speaker: einhard
text: …which he so disliked at first that he affirmed that he would not have entered the church on that day—though it was the chief festival of the church—if he could have foreseen the design of the Pope.
work: Life of Charlemagne, chapter 28
note: of the title of Emperor bestowed on Charlemagne in Rome on Christmas Day, 800

speaker: robert-boyle
text: I was quickly induc’d to think that the number of the Elements has been contended about by Philosophers with more earnestness then success.
work: The Sceptical Chymist (1661), part 1
note: spoken by Carneades, the sceptic of the dialogue

speaker: anaxagoras
text: The things that are in one world are not divided nor cut off from one another with a hatchet, neither the warm from the cold nor the cold from the warm.
work: Fragments (Burnet 8)

speaker: wilfrid-laurier
text: I am only too glad here to sink these differences, and to remember only the great services he has performed for our country…
work: Speech in the House of Commons on the death of Sir John A. Macdonald, 1891
note: as quoted in O. D. Skelton, The Day of Sir Wilfrid Laurier (1916)

speaker: chretien-de-troyes
text: Our books have informed us that the pre-eminence in chivalry and learning once belonged to Greece. Then chivalry passed to Rome, together with that highest learning which now has come to France.
work: Cligès, opening lines

speaker: louis-ix-of-france
text: …for there is no one whose life is not of as much value to him as mine to me; and maybe they will never get home at all.
work: Words to the sailors off Cyprus, 1254, on refusing to leave his damaged ship (Joinville, Memoirs)
note: as his friend Jean de Joinville, who was with him, recorded them

speaker: christiaan-huygens
text: I would believe then that those who love to know the Causes of things and who are able to admire the marvels of Light, will find some satisfaction in these various speculations regarding it…
work: Treatise on Light (1690), preface

speaker: thales-of-miletus
text: If we never do ourselves what we blame in others.
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 1
note: asked how men might live most virtuously and justly

speaker: georges-clemenceau
text: You pretend directly to construct the future, while we construct the man who will construct the future, and in so doing we are achieving a phenomenon much greater than your own.
work: Speech in the debate on socialism with Jean Jaurès, Chamber of Deputies, 1906
credit: tr. in The World's Famous Orations, ed. William Jennings Bryan, 1906 (translator not named)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: murasaki-shikibu
text: I listened, sitting beside him, and learned wonderfully fast, though he was sometimes slow and forgot. Father, who was devoted to study, regretted that I had not been a son…
work: Diary, 1008-1010, on learning Chinese beside her brother (in Diaries of Court Ladies of Old Japan)
credit: tr. Annie Shepley Omori and Kochi Doi, 1920

speaker: roger-williams
text: God requireth not an uniformity of religion to be enacted and enforced in any civil state; which enforced uniformity, sooner or later, is the greatest occasion of civil war, ravishing of conscience…
work: The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution for Cause of Conscience (1644), preface
note: in the modernised spelling of the 1848 Hanserd Knollys Society edition

speaker: giovanni-boccaccio
text: Algates, whoso goeth reading among these, let him leave those which offend and read those which divert.
work: The Decameron, the author's conclusion

speaker: pittacus
text: To do what one is doing at the moment well.
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 1
note: asked what was best

speaker: emilio-castelar
text: I said this because I know that, altho the Assembly, and the official authorities can make laws, they can not decree ideas or sentiments, those real and solid foundations of institutions.
work: Plea for a Republic, Spanish Constituent Cortes, 1869
credit: tr. in The World's Famous Orations, ed. William Jennings Bryan, 1906 (translator not named)
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: john-pym
text: The next great liberty is justice, whereby we are preserved from injuries in our persons and estates; from this is derived into the commonwealth, peace, and order, and safety; and when this is interrupted, confusion and danger are ready to overwhelm all.
work: Speech in the House of Commons on grievances, April 1640
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: thomas-more
text: They eat and drink out of vessels of earth or glass, which make an agreeable appearance, though formed of brittle materials; while they make their chamber-pots and close-stools of gold and silver…
work: Utopia, book 2, on the Utopians' gold
note: spoken by the traveller Raphael Hythloday in the dialogue

speaker: walter-raleigh
text: …having been a soldier, a captain, a sea captain, and a courtier, which are all places of wickedness and vice…
work: Speech on the scaffold, 29 October 1618
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: tao-yuanming
text: Long I lived checked by the bars of a cage: Now I have turned again to Nature and Freedom.
work: Returning to the Fields

speaker: henry-wadsworth-longfellow
text: Toiling,—rejoicing,—sorrowing, Onward through life he goes; Each morning sees some task begin, Each evening sees it close Something attempted, something done, Has earned a night's repose.
work: The Village Blacksmith (1840)

speaker: khosrow-i
text: …but the Romans will have the Persians as their own soldiers for the future, dispensing to them a fixed payment for their service…
work: To the Roman envoys, demanding a yearly payment, 540 (Procopius, History of the Wars, book 2)
note: Procopius' account

speaker: brasidas
text: I will accomplish what I wish in this war, or I will die for it.
work: Plutarch, Sayings of the Spartans (Moralia)
credit: tr. several hands, rev. William W. Goodwin, 1870
note: a letter to the ephors as he led out his army; Plutarch's collection of sayings

speaker: john-newton
text: It is always taken for granted, that they will attempt to gain their liberty, if possible.
work: Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade (1788), on the captives in the ships

speaker: hrotsvitha-of-gandersheim
text: I was like a person in a strange land wandering without a guide through a forest where the path is concealed by dense snow.
work: Preface to her verse history of the Emperor Otto I
note: on gathering the deeds of the emperor from hearsay

speaker: ulysses-s-grant
text: I am not aware of ever having used a profane expletive in my life; but I would have the charity to excuse those who may have done so, if they were in charge of a train of Mexican pack mules at the time.
work: Personal Memoirs (1885), on the war with Mexico

speaker: cyrus-the-younger
text: Not without a battle, be assured, shall the prize be won; if he be the son of Darius and Parysatis, and a brother of mine.
work: His answer to Clearchus, asked whether his brother the king would fight (Xenophon, Anabasis, book 1)
note: Xenophon's account

speaker: carl-linnaeus
text: I have a notion that Adam and Eve were giants, and that mankind from one generation to another, owing to poverty and other causes, have diminished in size.
work: Lachesis Lapponica, the journal of his tour in Lapland (1732)

speaker: darius-iii
text: …if our ruin be a debt that must be paid to the divine jealousy and the vicissitude of things, then I beseech you grant that no other man but Alexander may sit upon the throne of Cyrus.
work: His prayer after learning how Alexander had treated his family (Plutarch, Life of Alexander)
credit: tr. John Dryden and others, rev. A. H. Clough, 1859
note: Plutarch's account, which he says most historians give

speaker: mongke
text: I have sent my brothers away, and have exposed them to danger among foreign nations. Now, let it be seen what you will do, when I shall want to send you to increase our realm.
work: Words at his feast in Karakorum, June 1254
note: as the Franciscan envoy William of Rubruck, whom he received at Karakorum in 1254, recorded his words

speaker: susan-b-anthony
text: Yes, your honor, I have many things to say; for in your ordered verdict of guilty, you have trampled underfoot every vital principle of our government.
work: To the judge at her sentencing for voting, Canandaigua, 1873
note: from the trial record printed in the History of Woman Suffrage

speaker: shapur-ii
text: But I am at all times thoughtful to remember that, from my earliest youth, I have never done anything to repent of.
work: Letter to the emperor Constantius II, 358 (Ammianus Marcellinus, History, book 17)
note: the letter as Ammianus gives it

speaker: pierre-corneille
text: He who fears not death fears not threats.
work: Le Cid (1637), act 2
note: spoken by the Count, Chimène's father

speaker: faxian
text: …it was your former neglect of charity which brought you to your present state of destitution; and now, again, you wish to rob others.
work: To thieves who came to take the monks' rice (Memoirs of Eminent Monks, 519, in Legge's introduction)
note: as the Memoirs of Eminent Monks record it

speaker: john-ii-of-france
text: Sirs, strive not: lead me courteously, and my son, to my cousin the prince, and strive not for my taking, for I am so great a lord to make you all rich.
work: Words to the soldiers quarrelling over his capture, battle of Poitiers, 1356 (Froissart, Chronicles)
note: Froissart's account

speaker: pandita-ramabai
text: …who have done their best to keep women in a state of complete dependence and ignorance, vehemently deny that this has anything to do with the present degradation of the Hindu nation.
work: The High-Caste Hindu Woman (1887)

speaker: julian-emperor
text: …prosperity, however, does not always correspond to the wisdom of man's counsels, since the powers above reserve to themselves the regulation of results.
work: Ammianus Marcellinus, History, book 25
note: his last words to his officers, 363 CE; Ammianus' account

speaker: timur
text: I am not a man of blood; and God is my witness, that in all my wars I have never been the aggressor, and that my enemies have always been the authors of their own calamity.
work: To the doctors of the law at Aleppo, 1400 (in Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 65)
note: as Gibbon tells it, of a conqueror whose sacks of cities were notorious

speaker: jeremiah
text: …seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
work: Jeremiah 29:7, letter to the exiles in Babylon
note: the prophet speaking in the name of God
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: francois-fenelon
text: Ignorance is one of the causes of the ennui and discontent of young persons, and of the absence of all rational amusement.
work: Treatise on the Education of Daughters (1687)

speaker: robert-schumann
text: The object of art is not to produce riches. Become a great artist, and all other desirable accessories will fall to your lot.
work: Advice to Young Musicians (1850)

speaker: cambyses-ii
text: Do this, and then may your land bring you forth fruit abundantly, and your wives bear children, and your herds increase, and freedom be your portion for ever…
work: To the Persian nobles, dying, urging them to win back the throne from the Magi (Herodotus, Histories, book 3)
note: Herodotus's account
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: alcuin-of-york
text: Who does not fear? Who does not mourn this as if his fatherland itself was captured?
work: Letter to King Ethelred of Northumbria on the sack of Lindisfarne, 793

speaker: kabir
text: The moon shines in my body, but my blind eyes cannot see it…
work: Songs of Kabir

speaker: john-adams
text: Public virtues and political qualities, therefore, should be incessantly cherished in our children.
work: Letter to Abigail Adams, 29 October 1775

speaker: booker-t-washington
text: …we shall prosper in proportion as we learn to dignify and glorify common labour and put brains and skill into the common occupations of life…
work: Address at the Atlanta Cotton States Exposition, 1895 (Up from Slavery, chapter 14)

speaker: theocritus
text: Cicala to cicala is dear, and ant to ant, and hawks to hawks, but to me the Muse and song.
work: Idylls, 9

speaker: enrico-dandolo
text: If you will consent that I take the sign of the cross to guard and direct you, and that my son remain in my place to guard the land, then shall I go to live or die with you and with the pilgrims.
work: Speech in St Mark's, Venice, 1202 (Villehardouin, The Conquest of Constantinople)
note: Villehardouin's account; he was there

speaker: william-bradford-governor
text: …as one small candle may light a thousand, so the light enkindled here has shone to many, yea, in a sense, to our whole nation…
work: Of Plymouth Plantation, book 1
note: in Harold Paget's modern spelling (1909)

speaker: cao-pi
text: To sit idle is not my desire: Gladly enough would I go to my country’s aid.
work: The campaign against Wu

speaker: mark-twain
text: Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts. Broad, wholesome, charitable views of men and things can not be acquired by vegetating in one little corner of the earth all one’s lifetime.
work: The Innocents Abroad (1869), conclusion

speaker: samuel-de-champlain
text: …this is the art which in my early years won my love, and has induced me to expose myself almost all my life to the impetuous waves of the ocean.
work: Voyages (1613), address to the Queen Regent, on navigation
note: quoted in Edmund F. Slafter's memoir of Champlain

speaker: josephus
text: Dost thou send me to Nero? For why? Are Nero's successors till they come to thee still alive? Thou, O Vespasian, art Caesar and emperor, thou, and this thy son.
work: To Vespasian, as a prisoner, 67 (The Jewish War, book 3)
note: his own account of the prophecy he made; Vespasian became emperor two years later

speaker: william-tecumseh-sherman
text: By attempting to hold the roads, we will lose a thousand men each month, and will gain no result. I can make this march, and make Georgia howl!
work: Telegram to General Grant, 9 October 1864 (Memoirs, 1875)

speaker: thomas-cranmer
text: That next unto God you obey your king and queen willingly and gladly, without murmuring or grudging…
work: His last exhortation before his burning, Oxford, 21 March 1556
note: as Foxe recorded it

speaker: lope-de-vega
text: …since the crowd pays for the comedies, it is fitting to talk foolishly to it to satisfy its taste.
work: The New Art of Writing Plays (1609)

speaker: aristippus-of-cyrene
text: Send them both naked among strangers, and you will find out.
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 2
note: asked in what a wise man is superior to one who is not wise

speaker: jesus
text: He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.
work: John 8:7, to those who brought him a woman taken in adultery
note: as John's Gospel records it

speaker: william-morris

work: A Dream of John Ball (1888)
note: spoken by John Ball, the priest of the Peasants' Revolt of 1381

speaker: belisarius
text: Although your promise gave us to understand that your words would be brief and temperate, yet your discourse has been both long and not far from fraudulent in its pretensions.

speaker: william-pitt-the-younger
text: …we did not enter into this war for any purpose of ambition; our object was not to acquire, but to preserve; and in this sense, what we have gained by the war is, in one word, all that we should have lost without it…
work: Speech in the House of Commons on union with Ireland, 31 January 1799
note: on the war with revolutionary France

speaker: walter-bagehot
text: The object of such organisations is to create what may be called a cake of custom.
work: Physics and Politics (1872), ch. 2

speaker: olaf-ii-of-norway
text: The time may come, friend, when thou wilt command ships.
work: Words to his three-year-old half-brother (Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Saga of Olaf Haraldson)

speaker: ernest-renan

speaker: rabbi-akiva
text: Beloved is man, for he was created in the image (of God)…
work: Sayings of the Fathers (Pirke Avot) 3:18

speaker: pedro-calderon-de-la-barca

note: spoken by Prince Sigismund

speaker: multatuli
text: But if there should be amongst us any who neglect their duty for gain, who sell the Right for money, or who take away the buffalo from the poor, and bread from those who are hungry——who shall punish them?
work: Max Havelaar (1860), address to the chiefs of Lebak

speaker: w-b-yeats

work: The Stolen Child (1886)
