work: Letter on the discovery of Quintilian at St Gall, 1416
note: of the manuscript of the Roman writer Quintilian, found mouldering in the monastery

speaker: william-henry-harrison
text: The spirit of liberty is the sovereign balm for every injury which our institutions may receive.
work: Inaugural Address (1841)

speaker: lorenzo-de-medici
text: Midas treads a wearier measure: All he touches turns to gold: If there be no taste of pleasure, What's the use of wealth untold?
work: Song of Bacchus and Ariadne, a carnival song for Florence

speaker: increase-mather
text: It were better that ten suspected Witches should escape, than that one innocent Person should be Condemned; that is an old saying, and true…
work: Cases of Conscience Concerning Evil Spirits (1693)

speaker: cetshwayo
text: Have I not asked the English to allow me to wash my spears since the death of my father ‘Umpandi,’ and they have kept playing with me all this time, treating me like a child?
work: Message to the Governor of Natal, 1876
note: as printed in the British Blue Book and quoted by H. Rider Haggard (1882)

speaker: giovanni-pico-della-mirandola
text: I have set thee midmost the world, that thence thou mightest the more conveniently survey whatsoever is in the world.
work: Oration on the Dignity of Man, 1486
note: spoken by God to Adam in the Oration

speaker: alcuin-of-york
text: He who does not learn in youth does not teach in age.
work: Letter to the monks of Wearmouth and Jarrow, 793

speaker: william-penn
text: Governments, like clocks, go from the motion men give them; and as governments are made and moved by men, so by them they are ruined too. Wherefore governments rather depend upon men, than men upon governments.
work: Preface to the Frame of Government of Pennsylvania (1682)

speaker: bernard-of-clairvaux
text: But now especially is there need for it because holiness is rare, and it is plain that our age is lacking in men.
work: Life of St. Malachy of Armagh, preface

speaker: tewodros-ii
text: My father was mad, and though people often say that I am mad also; I never would believe it; but now I know it is true.
work: To the British envoys held at his court, 1866
note: as reported by Henry Blanc, one of the captives, in 1868

speaker: powhatan
text: I having seene the death of all my people thrice, and not any one living of these three generations but my selfe; I know the difference of Peace and Warre better then any in my Country.
work: To John Smith, 1609 (The Generall Historie of Virginia, 1624)
note: as John Smith recorded it

speaker: john-ross-cherokee-chief
text: We are denationalized; we are disfranchised. We are deprived of membership in the human family! We have neither land nor home, nor resting place that can be called our own.
work: Letter to the Senate and House of Representatives against the Treaty of New Echota, 1836

speaker: theodoric-the-great
text: War is a terrible thing, and a terrible risk. The long peace may have softened the hearts of your people, and your soldiers from want of practice may have lost the habit of working together on the battlefield.
work: Letter to Alaric II, king of the Visigoths, about 506 (Cassiodorus, Variae, book 3, letter 1)
note: a letter written in his name by his minister Cassiodorus, from the Variae

speaker: francis-drake
text: My Masters, I am a very bad orator, for my bringing up hath not been in learning…
work: Speech to his crew at Port St Julian, Patagonia, 1578
note: from the account of a member of the voyage, as quoted in William Wood, Elizabethan Sea-Dogs (1918)

speaker: robert-e-lee
text: I need not tell the survivors of so many hard-fought battles, who have remained steadfast to the last, that I have consented to this result from no distrust of them…
work: Farewell to the Army of Northern Virginia (General Order No. 9), 1865

speaker: sigurd-the-crusader
text: It appears to me much better for a chief who is to be the superior of other men, that he is conspicuous in a crowd, and strong and powerful in weapons above other men; easily seen, and easily known, where there are many together.
work: Words to his brother and co-king Eystein (Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Saga of Sigurd the Crusader)
note: from the two kings' contest of boasts over their ale, as Snorri Sturluson tells it

speaker: el-cid
text: Oh Martin Antolínez, thou art a good lance and leal. And if I live, hereafter I shall pay thee double rent, But gone is all my silver, and all my gold is spent.
work: The Lay of the Cid (Cantar de mio Cid), canto 1
credit: tr. R. Selden Rose and Leonard Bacon, 1919
note: spoken by the Cid in exile, in the epic composed about a century after his death

speaker: heinrich-heine
text: A drama will be enacted in Germany in comparison with which the French Revolution will appear a harmless idyl.
work: Religion and Philosophy in Germany (1834)

speaker: ignatius-of-loyola
text: Accept, O Lord, all my liberty, accept my memory, my understanding and my will. Thou hast given me all these powers; I restore them all to Thee, and I deliver them entirely into Thy hands that Thou mayest direct them.
work: Spiritual Exercises (1548), Contemplation to Obtain Divine Love

speaker: eugene-v-debs
text: Let the people everywhere take heart of hope, for the cross is bending, the midnight is passing, and joy cometh with the morning.
work: Statement to the court on being sentenced under the Espionage Act, Cleveland, September 1918
note: from the court stenographer's record

speaker: robert-emmet
text: When my country takes her place among the nations of the earth, then and not till then, let my epitaph be written.
work: Speech from the dock, Dublin, 19 September 1803, closing words
note: as printed in Speeches from the Dock (1867)

speaker: cassiodorus
text: The Sun, first of stars, seems to have lost his wonted light, and appears of a bluish colour. We marvel to see no shadows of our bodies at noon…
work: Letter to his deputy Ambrosius, on the famine of 536-537 (Variae, book 12, letter 25)
note: a letter he wrote as praetorian prefect of Italy, from his Variae

speaker: black-hawk-sauk-leader
text: How smooth must be the language of the whites, when they can make right look like wrong, and wrong like right.
work: Autobiography of Black Hawk (1833)
note: dictated to the interpreter Antoine LeClaire and edited by J. B. Patterson

speaker: leonardo-bruni
text: As Camillus was called the second founder of Rome, so may you receive the title of the second author of the works you have restored to the world.
work: Letter to Poggio Bracciolini on the recovered Quintilian, 1416
note: to the friend who had found the full text of the Roman writer Quintilian at St Gall

speaker: ruben-dario
text: Poets! Towers of God Made to resist the fury of the storms Like cliffs beside the ocean Or clouded, savage peaks! Masters of lightning! Breakwaters of eternity!
work: Poets! Towers of God (Cantos de vida y esperanza, 1905)
credit: tr. Thomas Walsh and Salomón de la Selva, 1916
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: theodoric-the-great
text: Away with this conflict, in which one of you will probably be utterly destroyed. Throw away the sword which you wield for my humiliation. By what right do I thus threaten you? By the right of a father and a friend.
work: Letter to Clovis, king of the Franks, about 506 (Cassiodorus, Variae, book 3, letter 4)
note: a letter written in his name by his minister Cassiodorus, from the Variae

speaker: robert-walpole
text: My great and principal crime is my long continuance in office; or, in other words, the long exclusion of those who now complain against me.
work: Speech in the House of Commons against the motion to remove him, 13 February 1741
note: as the parliamentary reports reconstructed it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: daniel-webster
text: I wish to speak to-day, not as a Massachusetts man, nor as a Northern man, but as an American…
work: The Seventh of March speech, United States Senate, 1850

speaker: poggio-bracciolini
text: So great is their mental torpor that nothing can rouse them to search after the works of excellent writers, by whose wisdom and learning mankind are taught the way to true happiness.
work: De Infelicitate Principum (On the Unhappiness of Princes)
note: of the popes and princes who would not spend on the search for lost books

speaker: cassiodorus
text: We have had a winter without storms, a spring without mildness, and a summer without heat.
work: Letter to his deputy Ambrosius, on the famine of 536-537 (Variae, book 12, letter 25)
note: a letter he wrote as praetorian prefect of Italy, from his Variae

speaker: ruben-dario
text: Come Lord, to make Thy glory, with lightnings on Thy brow! With trembling stars around Thee and cataclysmal woe, And bring Thy gifts of justice and peace and love below!
work: Song of Hope (Cantos de vida y esperanza, 1905)
credit: tr. Thomas Walsh and Salomón de la Selva, 1916
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: william-penn
text: Let men be good, and the government cannot be bad; if it be ill, they will cure it. But, if men be bad, let the government be never so good, they will endeavor to warp and spoil it to their turn.
work: Preface to the Frame of Government of Pennsylvania (1682)

speaker: william-henry-harrison
text: …the spirit of party, assuming to be that of liberty, is harsh, vindictive, and intolerant, and totally reckless as to the character of the allies which it brings to the aid of its cause.
work: Inaugural Address (1841)

speaker: giovanni-pico-della-mirandola
text: Thou shalt have power to decline unto the lower or brute creatures. Thou shalt have power to be reborn unto the higher, or divine, according to the sentence of thy intellect.
work: Oration on the Dignity of Man, 1486
note: spoken by God to Adam in the Oration

speaker: theodoric-the-great
text: What has man got a tongue for, if the armed hand is to settle all differences?
work: Letter to the people of Pannonia (Cassiodorus, Variae, book 3, letter 24)
note: a letter written in his name by his minister Cassiodorus, from the Variae

speaker: john-ross-cherokee-chief
text: Our property may be plundered before our eyes; violence may be committed on our persons; even our lives may be taken away, and there is none to regard our complaints.
work: Letter to the Senate and House of Representatives against the Treaty of New Echota, 1836

speaker: powhatan
text: What will it availe you to take that by force you may quickly have by love, or to destroy them that provide you food. What can you get by warre, when we can hide our provisions and fly to the woods?
work: To John Smith, 1609 (The Generall Historie of Virginia, 1624)
note: as John Smith recorded it

speaker: lorenzo-de-medici
text: Ladies and gay lovers young! Long live Bacchus, live Desire! Dance and play, let songs be sung; Let sweet Love your bosoms fire; In the future come what may!
work: Song of Bacchus and Ariadne, a carnival song for Florence

speaker: black-hawk-sauk-leader
text: Here for the first time, I touched the goose quill to the treaty not knowing, however, that, by the act I consented to give away my village. Had that been explained to me I should have opposed it and never would have signed their treaty…
work: Autobiography of Black Hawk (1833), on the treaty of 1816
note: dictated to the interpreter Antoine LeClaire and edited by J. B. Patterson

speaker: cassiodorus
text: Then was paper discovered, and therewith was eloquence made possible.
work: Letter to Joannes, in praise of paper (Variae, book 11, letter 38)
note: a letter he wrote as praetorian prefect of Italy, from his Variae

speaker: heinrich-heine
text: …freedom is a new religion, the religion of our age. If Christ is not the God of this religion, he is still one of its high-priests, and his name shines consolingly in the hearts of its children.
work: English Fragments (1828), The Liberation

speaker: robert-walpole
text: Have I ever been suspected of being corrupted? A strange phenomenon, a corrupter himself not corrupt!
work: Speech in the House of Commons against the motion to remove him, 13 February 1741
note: as the parliamentary reports reconstructed it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: daniel-webster
text: Secession! Peaceable secession! Sir, your eyes and mine are never destined to see that miracle. The dismemberment of this vast country without convulsion! The breaking up of the fountains of the great deep without ruffling the surface!
work: The Seventh of March speech, United States Senate, 1850

speaker: leonardo-bruni
text: Through you we now possess Quintilian entire; before we only boasted of the half of him, and that defective and corrupt in text.
work: Letter to Poggio Bracciolini on the recovered Quintilian, 1416
note: to the friend who had found the full text of the Roman writer Quintilian at St Gall

speaker: theodoric-the-great
text: The true mark of civilitas is the observance of law. It is this which makes life in communities possible, and which separates man from the brutes.
work: Letter to the Jews of Genoa (Cassiodorus, Variae, book 4, letter 33)
note: a letter written in his name by his minister Cassiodorus, from the Variae

speaker: william-penn
text: Any government is free to the people under it (whatever be the frame) where the laws rule, and the people are a party to those laws, and more than this is tyranny, oligarchy, or confusion.
work: Preface to the Frame of Government of Pennsylvania (1682)

speaker: robert-emmet
text: I am going to my cold and silent grave—my lamp of life is nearly extinguished—my race is run—the grave opens to receive me, and I sink into its bosom.
work: Speech from the dock, Dublin, 19 September 1803
note: as printed in Speeches from the Dock (1867)

speaker: john-ross-cherokee-chief
text: The instrument in question is not the act of our Nation; we are not parties to its covenants; it has not received the sanction of our people.
work: Letter to the Senate and House of Representatives against the Treaty of New Echota, 1836

speaker: black-hawk-sauk-leader
text: With us it is a custom to visit the graves of our friends and keep them in repair for many years. The mother will go alone to weep over the grave of her child.
work: Autobiography of Black Hawk (1833)
note: dictated to the interpreter Antoine LeClaire and edited by J. B. Patterson

speaker: powhatan
text: Thinke you I am so simple, not to know it is better to eate good meate, lye well, and sleepe quietly with my women and children, laugh and be merry with you, have copper, hatchets, or what I want being your friend…
work: To John Smith, 1609 (The Generall Historie of Virginia, 1624)
note: as John Smith recorded it

speaker: robert-walpole
text: …yet I will not shrink from the responsibility which attaches to the post I have the honor to hold…
work: Speech in the House of Commons against the motion to remove him, 13 February 1741
note: as the parliamentary reports reconstructed it
licence: Public domain; Wikisource transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

speaker: heinrich-heine
text: Paris is the New Jerusalem, and the Rhine is the Jordan which separates the land of Freedom from the land of the Philistines.
work: English Fragments (1828), The Liberation

speaker: william-penn
text: …for liberty without obedience is confusion, and obedience without liberty is slavery.
work: Preface to the Frame of Government of Pennsylvania (1682)

speaker: daniel-webster
text: …and there was with them from that moment to the end of the war, what I hope will remain with them for ever, one cause, one country, one heart.
work: Address at the laying of the cornerstone of the Bunker Hill Monument, 1825

speaker: black-hawk-sauk-leader
text: The changes of fortune and vicissitudes of war made you my conqueror. When my last resources were exhausted, my warriors worn down with long and toilsome marches, we yielded, and I became your prisoner.
work: Autobiography of Black Hawk (1833), dedication to General Henry Atkinson
note: dictated to the interpreter Antoine LeClaire and edited by J. B. Patterson

speaker: john-ross-cherokee-chief
text: We are overwhelmed! Our hearts are sickened, our utterance is paralized, when we reflect on the condition in which we are placed…
work: Letter to the Senate and House of Representatives against the Treaty of New Echota, 1836
